a79.speaker: Nampak Zimbabwe (company statement accompanying financial results)
a79.speech: Reported a significant drop in key profit margins due to increased competition, which is eroding its market share. The informalisation of the retail sector and disruptions to the route-to-market also contributed to declining demand from some customer segments.

a99.speaker: AMDISS (Association for Media Development in South Sudan) (press release)
a99.speech: Is pleased to announce the successful completion of the renovation and handing over of two radio studios at Singaita FM in Kapoeta. Said the renovation marks a significant enhancement in the broadcasting capabilities of Singaita FM, thanks to the dedicated efforts of Radio Technician Stephen Phillip. Said this renovation project is part of the SIMA initiative and was made possible through the generous support of USAID, in collaboration with IREX. Extended gratitude to Stephen Phillip for his technical expertise and dedication, as well as to USAID and IREX for their unwavering support in making this project a success.

a137.speaker: Omar Njie, artisanal fisherman at the Tanji fish landing site
a137.speech: Said the fisherfolk have experienced a sharp decline in their catches in the last few years ; believes a significant contributor is overfishing caused by Senegalese in Gambian waters.

a137.speaker: Gambia National Association of Artisanal Fisheries
a137.speech: According to the association, Gambia and Senegal signed a fishing agreement in 2017, renewed in 2023, without the participation of the country’s artisanal fishermen.

a137.speaker: Study (cited)
a137.speech: Study establishes that the suppliers of the 3 fish meals in the Gambia are Senegalese.

a137.speaker: Industry experts and local fishermen
a137.speech: Said the 4-year fishing agreement renewed in September 2023 gives Senegal far more advantage over Gambia.

a137.speaker: Media reports
a137.speech: According to media reports, the Senegalese fishermen who come to Gambia to fish in the country’s waters and the ones who supply the fish meals during the night fight fishing period are not operating under the agreement.

a137.speaker: Fisheries official who does not want to be named (anonymous)
a137.speech: “We are already seeing scarcity of fish in the Gambia” ; “The signed agreement is not reciprocal.”

a137.speaker: Experts
a137.speech: Said that with article one of the agreement allowing fishermen to land their catch in either country, and Senegalese having the higher buyer power, this leaves Gambian consumers vulnerable.

a137.speaker: Musa S. Drammeh, Gambian fisheries minister
a137.speech: Told lawmakers in July that Senegalese fishermen in Gambia’s waters take their catches home but attributed this to lack of landing ports in the country.

a137.speaker: Ousman Njie, boat owner at Tanji
a137.speech: “We are experiencing a very significant drop in our catch” ; “We pay tax, still we are not protected by our government. And our income has truly declined.”

a137.speaker: World Bank
a137.speech: According to the World Bank, about 6 in every 10 Gambians live below a dollar a day.

a137.speaker: Mamodou Sarr, artisanal fisherman in Tanji
a137.speech: Said the price hikes influenced by scarcity of fish will make fish unaffordable for the majority of Gambians.

a137.speaker: Musa Drammeh, Gambian fisheries minister
a137.speech: In July 2023 refuted claims that the presence of Senegalese boats in Gambian water is a leading cause of fish scarcity in the country; said the agreement has paved the way for both countries to fish in each other’s waters: “We have only 137 artisanal fishing vessels from Senegal as far as our records are concerned.”

a956.speaker: Fingile Makgalemele, corporate communications manager, Botswana Examinations Council (BEC)
a956.speech: explained: “This is an international paper, so there is no way it can be moved because candidates in other countries would have written the exam already, so it is only proper for local candidates to sit for the paper on that date.”

a1071.speaker: Bertha Bangara-Chikadza, president of the Economics Association of Malawi (Ecama) and economics lecturer at the University of Malawi
a1071.speech: Noting that the country's economy is teetering on the brink of collapse, said the new government should focus on stabilising the economy and cut any unnecessary expenditure, minimise leakages and wastage by enforcing austerity measures; she outlined five areas of focus, namely the need to tackle inflation, boost exports to stabilise forex reserves, restore fiscal discipline, prioritise productive investments, and implement the Malawi 2063 (MW2063). "It is time to rebuild and the government should lead by cutting unnecessary expenditures and reduce borrowing. For these proposed solutions to work, there is a need for concerted efforts from the government, the private sector, and development partners. However, based on current trends in official development assistance, the country needs to focus more on local solutions than relying on donor support for its development."

a1071.speaker: Bertha Bangara-Chikadza, president of the Economics Association of Malawi (Ecama)
a1071.speech: Said that since inflation is primarily driven by food pressures and imported inflation that comes with lack of forex in formal financial markets, short-term interventions should focus on strengthening agricultural production to stabilise food availability; she also called on the new government to allocate resources strategically and effectively to support the MW2063 commitments and avoid deviations from the main development agenda.

a1071.speaker: Benedicto Kondowe, executive director of the Civil Society Education Coalition (Csec)
a1071.speech: Said the new government must view education as Malawi's survival strategy, adding Malawians want to see improved resource allocation to the sector to facilitate improved outcomes on quality education standards; he said the new government should implement free secondary education, abolish examination fees, provide food in universities, improve teachers' welfare, and decongest classrooms by constructing more blocks. "In short, the new government must view education not as a political slogan, but as Malawi's survival strategy. The rollout of free secondary education and the removal of examination fees must be matched with bold investments in quality, equity, and accountability so that no child is left behind."

a1071.speaker: George Jobe, executive director of the Malawi Health Equity Network (Mhen)
a1071.speech: Called for adequate funding to address various challenges in the health sector and urged government to move with speed in putting in place a national health fund as promised in the DPP manifesto, which should be sustained through innovative domestic resource mobilisation strategies.

a1071.speaker: Maziko Matemba, executive director of the Health Rights Education Programme (Hrep)
a1071.speech: Called for adequate resources in health facilities, including drugs, human resource, and equipment: "There will be need for increased funding to the health sector, especially now that donor support is shrinking. Government should also ensure that donors that are still supporting us do not stop supporting the country."

a1071.speaker: Annabel Mtalimanja, chairperson of the Malawi Electoral Commission
a1071.speech: On Wednesday declared DPP presidential candidate Peter Mutharika as winner of the presidential election in the September 16 General Election.

a1138.speaker: Jeffrey Frankel, professor of Capital Formation and Growth at Harvard University and research associate at the US National Bureau of Economic Research (commentary provided by Project Syndicate)
a1138.speech: Warned that the shift in US policy risks reversing these gains, potentially to the strategic advantage of emerging global powers like China. He argues that aid efforts have fortified US soft power post-Cold War, enabling global leadership and promoting global stability, and that "whatever the limitations of foreign aid in the past, it is clear that Trump's destructive approach is making things far worse."

a1138.speaker: Joni Mitchell, singer
a1138.speech: Sang the line "Don't it always seem to go, that you don't know what you've got 'til it's gone" in 1970, lamenting the destruction of the environment.

a1138.speaker: Dambisa Moyo and William Easterly, scholars
a1138.speech: Argue that foreign aid does more harm than good, believing that foreign aid has a negligible impact.

a1138.speaker: Paul Collier, economist
a1138.speech: Insists that foreign aid is useful, especially when certain conditions are met.

a1138.speaker: A 2018 survey
a1138.speech: Showed that a substantial majority of people in rich countries believed that the child-mortality rate in poor countries had either risen or stayed the same over the previous 20 years; in fact, child mortality had been halved. And a whopping 80pc of people in rich countries believed that the share of people in extreme poverty had either plateaued or risen, even though it fell steeply from 1990 to 2013.

a1144.speaker: UNAIDS, Global AIDS Update 2025 report (released in July)
a1144.speech: Listed South Africa, Uganda, Botswana, Tanzania and Togo among at least 25 countries across the world that are committing to increase domestic budgets for HIV prevention and care. "In 2025, the HIV financing architecture has undergone unprecedented changes. Most notably, the freeze and uncertainty surrounding PEPFAR's funding commitments." ; UNAIDS statistics show that at the end of 2024, US$18.7 billion was available for the AIDS response in low- and middle-income countries, just 17% below the US$21.9 billion needed annually by 2030; around 52% was from domestic sources, with local funding increased by 2.2% in 2024, the first rise since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. "This is promising, but not sufficient to replace the scale of international funding in countries that are heavily reliant," the report warns.

a1144.speaker: United States Senate
a1144.speech: In mid-July, the U.S. Senate objected to major funding cuts, with efforts to claw back an additional US$400 million already appropriated to the PEPFAR program.

a1144.speaker: 2025 UNCTAD report
a1144.speech: Projects that development assistance to Africa will plummet to just US$24 billion by year end, down from US$80 billion in 2021, a staggering 70% drop and the sharpest decline in decades.

a1144.speaker: South African government
a1144.speech: Said the funds will be used to support a centralized patient information system, chronic medicine distribution, and medicine stock surveillance.

a1144.speaker: Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General
a1144.speech: At the 13th International AIDS Society Conference (IAS 2025) in Kigali, Rwanda, confirmed this transition, citing it as a pivotal moment for Africa. "Many health ministers and leaders have told me that they see this crisis as an opportunity to leave behind the dependency and move toward sustainable self-reliance by mobilizing domestic resources." ; "We cannot let that progress slip away. Governments, scientists, civil society, and affected communities must stand together to uphold those gains and shape a new sustainable path rooted in shared responsibility and equity."

a1144.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a1144.speech: Launched a new long-acting injectable antiretroviral, lenacapavir (LEN), designed to replace costlier daily oral treatments, encouraging governments to adopt rapid HIV testing kits to reduce the burden of "complex, costly procedures." According to WHO, 1.3 million people contracted HIV in 2024 across the world, with the highest burden borne by sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, people who inject drugs, incarcerated individuals, and adolescents; Africa had the highest share of new infections at 490,000 and the highest share of women and girls at 63% against the world average of 45%.

a1144.speaker: Africa CDC report, 'Africa's Health Financing in a New Era' (published April 2025)
a1144.speech: Most African nations continue to allocate less than 10% of their national budgets to health, with about 30 African countries allocating as little as 5-7%, far short of the 15% target set under the 2001 Abuja Declaration; only Rwanda, Botswana and Cabo Verde have consistently met or exceeded the goal. "Despite decades of advocacy, African countries continue to allocate insufficient domestic resources to health, undermining progress toward health equity and system resilience."

a1144.speaker: Africa CDC
a1144.speech: Called for a new wave of political and financial commitment, including updated national health development and financing plans, and the establishment of innovative funding mechanisms such as health insurance schemes, sin taxes, and solidarity levies.

a1189.speaker: Liberia News Agency (LINA) (press release)
a1189.speech: According to a LINA release, the event is part of LINA's broader strategy to make government public relations more engaging and bring decision-makers closer to young people; the central focus of the discussion is "The ARREST Agenda: What's in it for young people?" - ensuring that Liberia's youth understand how government policies, particularly in times of economic transition, impact their future. The public, including youth groups, community leaders, government representatives as well as student organizations are invited, and the session will be live streamed and published across all major social media platforms.

a1199.speaker: Internal State Department cable (ALDAC) excerpts reviewed by Reuters
a1199.speech: Under the new arrangement, all U.S. overseas missions should consult with PRM on foreign disaster declarations, said the cable. "With approval from PRM based on established criteria for international disaster assistance, up to $100,000 can be issued to support the initial response," it continued. "Additional resources may be forthcoming based on established humanitarian need" in consultation with other State Department offices. ; One cable excerpt said that in the event of an overseas disaster, PRM may call on what's left of USAID's Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance to mobilize the remnants of its staff "to provide the most efficient and effective response."

a1199.speaker: State Department (non-response)
a1199.speech: The State Department did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

a1199.speaker: Source familiar with the matter (anonymous)
a1199.speech: confirmed on condition of anonymity the authenticity of the excerpts. Only 20 experts out of the roughly 525 who did the work at USAID's Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance and its Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Relief are being hired by PRM, the source said. But, the source continued, the number is far from adequate and the PRM leadership has "no concept of how to" mount responses to major overseas disasters. "They do not understand disaster response," said the source.

a1199.speaker: Jeremy Konyndyk, former director of the Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Relief and president of Refugees International
a1199.speech: "It's a joke. It's ridiculous. PRM is not an operational entity. They do important stuff but this is not what they do." ; Konyndyk warned that with the approaching Caribbean hurricane season the U.S. can no longer mobilize the world-leading Disaster Assistance Response Teams (DARTs) it once could to help with serious disasters on this side of the globe. "The mechanics of how DARTs work cannot be replicated in PRM. They are just trying to create a Potemkin DART."

a1199.speaker: Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State
a1199.speech: has rejected criticism of the administration response to the earthquake in Myanmar. He said it was a difficult place to work, the military junta does not like the U.S. and it was unfair that the U.S. has provided most international humanitarian aid.

a1199.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a1199.speech: say the Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration lacks the knowhow and personnel for the role; USAID's gutting has already led to what many experts called the administration's late and inadequate response to a serious earthquake in Myanmar on March 25.

a1208.speaker: Ghana AIDS Commission (GAC)
a1208.speech: revealed that more than half of the people living with HIV/AIDS have not sought the life-saving antiretroviral therapy treatment. In its 2024 national and sub-national HIV estimates and projections, the commission reports that 334,721 people living with HIV, accounting for 47 per cent of that population, are currently on antiretroviral therapy treatment, with 52.6 per cent without treatment. The commission has described the situation as "alarming", warning of its potential to derail national efforts to control the epidemic. The current situation, it said, had left the lives of the entire population, including non-HIV patients, at risk.

a1208.speaker: Isaiah Doe Kwao, Director of Research, Monitoring and Evaluation at the Ghana AIDS Commission
a1208.speech: said the figures fell short of the global 95-95-95 targets set by the United Nations programme for HIV and AIDS, UNAIDS, for 95 per cent of people living with HIV to know their status, 95 per cent of those diagnosed to be on treatment and 95 per cent of those on treatment to achieve viral suppression. Breaking down the statistics, Mr Kwao explained that 15,290 new HIV infections were recorded in 2024 alone, and that although 12,614 AIDS-related deaths were recorded, an estimated 12,358 deaths were prevented due to access to treatment. He said the data underscored the urgent need to expand access to antiretroviral therapy treatment. Mr Kwao stated that women and children continued to bear a disproportionate burden, with 68.5 per cent (10,303) of new infections occurring in females and 5.4 per cent (1,243) occurring in children under 15. He remarked that although Ghana boasts that 99.3 per cent of HIV-positive mothers now receive prevention of mother-to-child transmission, more needed to be done to ensure effective follow-up and treatment to reduce the figures. He added, however, that the records for males were 4,987, while adults aged 15 and older recorded 11,289 out of the 15,290 new cases.

a1208.speaker: Nana Oye Bampoe Addo, Deputy Chief of Staff
a1208.speech: said issues such as misinformation, disinformation, stigma, discrimination, individual economic challenges, inadequate lifesaving services and recent funding cuts had contributed to derail progress. "Regardless, we are determined to ensure sustained domestic financing, including the recent suspension of USAID's international funding programme; integrate HIV priorities into broader health and development strategies, and adopt innovative, data-driven approaches to enhance service delivery. No one should be left behind in our HIV response," she emphasised. She also cautioned that every HIV-positive person who was not on treatment was one step closer to advanced illness and AIDS-related death, which she said was unacceptable. She stressed that, especially in present times, there should not be such a wide treatment gap.

a1208.speaker: Nana Oye Bampoe Addo, Deputy Chief of Staff
a1208.speech: As Ghana prepares to host the 2025 International Conference on AIDS and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in Africa (ICASA), the Deputy Chief of Staff called on stakeholders, government institutions, health workers, donors, researchers, community advocates and civil society leaders to reflect deeply on the findings from these estimates and turn them into purposeful action.

a1404.speaker: Somali authorities
a1404.speech: Said Somali police on Tuesday publicly burned 250 cartons of drugs in Mogadishu after seizing them during an attempted illegal import.

a1404.speaker: Maj. Abdifitah Adan Hassan, Somali police spokesperson
a1404.speech: Told reporters the drugs were confiscated at Mogadishu Port and Aden Adde International Airport following heightened surveillance of suspected smuggling activities. He said the destruction was carried out under an order from the Banadir Regional Court. He warned that security agencies are intensifying monitoring and surveillance at all entry points — including ports, airports and border crossings — to deter smuggling attempts, and urged individuals involved in the illegal trade to stop, saying authorities will take strict action.

a1404.speaker: Banadir Regional Court (order)
a1404.speech: Ordered the destruction of the seized drugs.

a1475.speaker: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), recent analysis
a1475.speech: confirms what Somalis have known for years: this country faces extreme environmental fragility and is among the world's most vulnerable to climate-induced displacement.

a1475.speaker: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) data
a1475.speech: In 2021–22, only 5.3% of climate-related development finance from OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) members reached countries with extreme fragility. Overall, 25.6% went to countries experiencing high fragility.

a1475.speaker: Liban Obsiye, Head of the Strategic Economic Unit of the Somali Ministry of Finance (opinion piece)
a1475.speech: argues that climate resilience is key to peacebuilding in Somalia: "To get ahead of the crisis, Somalia's government is taking notable strides, not only through force against international terrorists, but through reconciliation, awareness and broad-based intercommunal dialogue." ; writes that Somalia's climate agenda must be fully aligned with its economic vision, captured in Vision 2060 and the National Transformation Plan (NTP) 2025-2029, that quick fixes and emergency aid will not resolve structural fragilities and vulnerability traps, and that countries on the climate front lines need financing that is faster, fairer, and fit for purpose.

a1475.speaker: Somali government
a1475.speech: is accelerating efforts to access climate financing from all available sources, including the major vertical funds; a new climate finance architecture, anchored on the National Climate Fund within the Ministry of Finance, is reshaping how the country plans and manages climate resources. The NTP directs efforts to identify, allocate, and monitor funding that tackles the roots of conflict by investing in climate-smart agriculture, water management, fisheries, and pastoral supply chains.

a1622.speaker: The New York Times
a1622.speech: Reported on Thursday that Elon Musk, an ally of US President-elect Donald Trump, met on Monday with Iran's ambassador to the UN in order to "ease tensions" between Tehran and the United States.

a1622.speaker: Two anonymous Iranian sources (cited by the New York Times)
a1622.speech: Specified that the meeting of more than an hour, at a secret location in New York, between the billionaire and Amir Saeid Iravani had been "positive" and represented "good news."

a1622.speaker: Iran's mission to the United Nations
a1622.speech: Asked by AFP, it said it had "no comment."

a1622.speaker: Donald Trump's team
a1622.speech: Did not confirm the meeting either.

a1622.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a1622.speech: Confirmed this week his campaign promise by appointing Elon Musk, the richest man on the planet, to head a new Commission on Government Efficiency.

a1622.speaker: Iran
a1622.speech: Sent Donald Trump a signal of openness last week by calling on him to adopt a new policy towards it, after Washington accused Tehran of involvement in a plot to assassinate the US president-elect.

a1622.speaker: Washington (United States government)
a1622.speech: Accused Tehran of involvement in a plot to assassinate the US president-elect.

a1624.speaker: Students from various public schools (some of the students)
a1624.speech: According to them, the MCC had extended invitations to their schools, inviting them for the event, but upon arrival only a select few were allowed entry, while the rest were told that the hall was at full capacity, leaving them disappointed and confused.

a1624.speaker: K.B.K. Sando Massaquoi (William V.S. Tubman High School), Emmanuel Dóe (D. Twe Memorial High School) and Moses S. Yorgbor (Monrovia Central High School), students
a1624.speech: Told the NEW DAWN that they never expected to be treated in such a manner; they expressed frustration over the lack of communication regarding the limited space, further lamenting that since being denied entry they had been sitting outside with no one offering them even a bottle of water: "We can't just go home; we have to wait for our colleagues so that we can leave together."

a1624.speaker: Another student (unnamed)
a1624.speech: "This isn't fair! If they had a specific number of people they needed, they should have informed our administration ahead of time. Now, they're rejecting people, and it's really shameful."

a1624.speaker: John Charuk Siafa, Monrovia City Mayor
a1624.speech: At the Ministry of Information, Cultural Affairs, and Tourism's regular press briefing on Tuesday, February 4, 2025, extended an open invitation to all Liberians, including students, journalists, civil society organizations, local and international businesses and community leaders, to discuss challenges and strategies for shaping Monrovia's future.

a1624.speaker: MCC officers at the gate
a1624.speech: When asked about the situation, stated that the venue was too small to accommodate the number of attendees, and further explained that for this reason they had been instructed to accept only individuals with passes into the building.

a1692.speaker: Manuel Stofleth-Mitterer, Austrian architect and property developer, IN-US.world
a1692.speech: Looks over "The Health Farm" with pride and sums up his life motto: "Without health, everything is nothing."

a1692.speaker: Angelika Mitterer, Austrian architect, IN-US.world
a1692.speech: Raves about The Gambia as she did on the first day: "For me, The Gambia is a very warm-hearted place. Colourful, loud and full of life. The open and friendly people here just make my life in The Gambia so much more beautiful."

a1763.speaker: Evelyn Anite, Ugandan State Minister for Privatisation and Investment
a1763.speech: Announced that through the National Medical Stores (NMS), the government will procure health supplies from local manufacturers to boost their growth and reduce reliance on imports. Anite made the remarks while touring Mavid Pharmaceutical Industries in Bilongo, Kajjansi, Wakiso District.

a1763.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bukenya, Head of Pharmacy at Mavid Pharmaceuticals
a1763.speech: Urged the government to lower taxes on raw materials, saying this would help reduce the final cost of medicine for Ugandans.

a2041.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council (NPC)
a2041.speech: Announced on Friday, December 6 that WANEP and the NPC have deployed 510 accredited observers to 276 medium- to high-risk areas across the constituencies, while revealing the establishment of the Election Situation Room (ESR) to monitor the 2024 elections ; "Five hundred and ten accredited observers, including 319 observers from WANEP, have been deployed mainly to 276 prioritised 'very high-risk' to 'Medium-risk' constituencies across Ghana's 16 regions" ; said the observers would use a checklist comprising 63 questions, divided into six forms, to monitor voting processes within their assigned areas ; said the ESR, with support from RERGs established in 11 regions, would undertake preventive actions across the country, and that the 11 regions were selected on the basis of their threat analysis conducted earlier in the year.

a2041.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council (NPC)
a2041.speech: Said in May this year that the NPC and WANEP, in partnership with ECOWAS, ECONEC and UNOWAS, launched the National Election Response Group (NERG) and Regional Election Response Group (RERG), and said the NERG/RERG was made up of prominent individuals representing key state and non-state institutions to prevent and mitigate violence associated with elections: "This collaborative effort highlights NPC and WANEP's commitment to promoting peace, security and successful elections in Ghana by providing timely information and strategic response mechanisms."

a2041.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council (NPC)
a2041.speech: Said reports would be submitted through a Geospatial Information System (GIS) designed for that purpose and that additional updates would be received via dedicated WhatsApp channels and phone calls between the situation room and field observers ; "134 personnel, including youth, women, elections experts, and eminent persons have been mobilised to operationalise the ESR with the support of resource persons from other West African countries, from December 6-8, this year" ; said a team of fact checkers from the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJIO) and West Africa FactSpace would support the ESR in validating sensitive incidents and other social media posts before being released to the public.

a2041.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council (NPC)
a2041.speech: Said while the NPC and WANEP hotspot mapping reports identified 203 "very-high to medium-risk areas nationwide based on their specific election security indicators, the EC had reportedly identified 7,250 flashpoints nationwide, and mentioned some of the challenges identified to include an environment of mistrust and suspicions of key state institutions by a section of the citizenry, mistrust and suspicions among political actors, negative media reportage and social media vulnerabilities, including information disorders.

a2041.speaker: Rev. Dr Ernest Adu-Gyamfi, Chairman of the National Peace Council (NPC)
a2041.speech: Said given the challenges raised, the EC was encouraged to continue to maintain frequent communication with stakeholders and the general public throughout the electoral process: "The National Election Security Taskforce is encouraged to continue to uphold the principles of neutrality, impartiality and professionalism in the discharge of their duties, the National Communication Authority (NCA), the Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) and the National Media Commission (NMC) should encourage their members to respect the ethics of the journalist profession and refrain from disseminating any information that could exacerbate tension, the general public should verify before sharing information on social media."

a2154.speaker: World Bank (report)
a2154.speech: Projects economic growth of 5.7% for the current year, driven mainly by the resumption of oil exports; warns against excessive dependence on oil: "While oil production and exports should increase public revenues, they will also amplify the possibility of growth", stressing that it is a limited resource ; recommends that Niger diversify its economy and invest massively in the education sector, and proposes financing this additional spending by improving the efficiency of public spending on education and strengthening the mobilisation of domestic revenue ; stresses that the projected fall in the extreme poverty rate to 42.5% by the end of 2026 rests on several assumptions, notably a good agricultural season and effective management of oil revenues.

a2154.speaker: Mahama Samir Bandaogo, senior economist at the World Bank
a2154.speech: "It is crucial to focus on improving productivity by investing in particular in the field of education."

a2265.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a2265.speech: Considers that Kaïs Saïed is not sending him the right signals -- non-respect of the fundamentals of democracy, support for the Palestinian cause ; These signals, considered hostile to Washington, convinced Donald Trump to remove Tunis from his regional priorities.

a2265.speaker: The White House
a2265.speech: Criticises President Kaïs Saïed for his distancing from the fundamentals of democracy and his pro-Palestinian positioning, judged to be too assertive.

a2265.speaker: Washington / Trump administration
a2265.speech: Now conditions its support on a clear return to the democratic path and on a more conciliatory alignment on certain strategic Middle East issues.

a2265.speaker: Tunisian authorities (no response)
a2265.speech: The Tunisian authorities remained silent in the face of the new tariff barrier, which nevertheless risks weakening an agri-food sector already weakened by drought and declining competitiveness.

a2265.speaker: Kaïs Saïed, President of Tunisia
a2265.speech: Entrenched in a sovereignist posture and displaying unfailing solidarity with the Palestinian cause, chooses for the moment not to shift his position.

a2277.speaker: African energy and finance ministers (Mission 300 Africa Energy Summit panel)
a2277.speech: Welcomed an ambitious new partnership to transform the continent's power sector at the Mission 300 Africa Energy Summit in Dar es Salaam on January 27, while highlighting their countries' distinct paths toward achieving universal access to electricity. ; Ministers representing South Africa, Zambia, Kenya, Cote d'Ivoire and Nigeria emphasized that while each nation faces unique challenges, success will require political leadership, policy reforms, and private sector participation.

a2277.speaker: Dr. Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, South Africa's Minister of Electricity
a2277.speech: Noted that under Mission 300, "every country will be able to carve its own unique path." He outlined three key priorities for the electricity sector: affordability and accessibility, a just and affordable transition, and regional interconnectivity, noting that "essentially, we see ourselves as a connection of countries that are connected by these regional pools."

a2277.speaker: Mamadou Sangafowa-Coulibaly, Cote d'Ivoire's Minister of Mines, Petroleum and Energy
a2277.speech: Highlighted his country's role in regional power trade: "There are six countries with whom we exchange electricity and to which we export electricity." Referencing the country's gas and hydro power potential, he described plans to double the quantity of energy exports to the country's neighbours by 2030. He however also emphasized payment challenges in cross-border electricity trade: "The electricity that we export, we are not always paid for it, which of course does create a huge challenge."

a2277.speaker: Dr. Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambia's Minister of Finance
a2277.speech: Highlighted his country's urgent need to expand power generation to support ambitious mining sector growth. "We are on a trajectory to triple copper production in the next ten years," he said. "That requires electricity. We must minimize dependence on hydroelectric power and diversify our energy sources." He emphasized that recent reforms have created attractive opportunities for private investors and invited them to "come to Zambia and invest in energy."

a2277.speaker: Wale Edun, Nigeria's Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy
a2277.speech: Highlighted the country's progress in attracting private investment: "Since the regulation of the sector, we've had 150 mini-grids set up and a million standalone solar connections in recent times." Drawing a parallel with the mobile telecommunications sector, he noted: "There was a time people would say that telephones are for the wealthy, the preserve of the rich. And now everybody has one." He stressed that a similar "revolution" needed to take place in Nigeria's energy sector.

a2277.speaker: Opiyo Wandayi, Kenya's Minister of Energy and Petroleum
a2277.speech: Stressed the importance of partnerships: "To achieve such an ambitious plan that is bound to benefit millions of people, it is not possible to do it alone. The principle of partnership is at the center of our strategy in terms of not only ensuring universal access to electricity but also in implementing our clean cooking strategy."

a2277.speaker: Dr. Kevin Kariuki, African Development Bank Vice President for Power, Energy, Climate and Green Growth
a2277.speech: Opened the panel discussion by setting out Mission 300's ambitious scope: "We shall provide fast and energy-efficient solutions to 300 million people across Africa. This effort is targeted at development. It is difficult, it is challenging, but cost-effective outcomes can play a crucial role."

a2277.speaker: Dr. Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
a2277.speech: Set the tone for the summit during the opening session: "This is not a talking summit. We can do megawatts of talk all we want, but it's going to be the megawatts of power that we deliver that make this an action-driven summit. We need everybody - the heads of state, the private sector, the multilateral development banks, civil society - all of us working together. It's not about us. It's about those who are not here - the small business enterprises trying to simply have access to electricity to run our economies."

a2379.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2379.speech: Says that the tariffs proposed by Mozal for the consumption of energy from the Cahora Bassa Hydroelectric plant would lead the power generation company to collapse; guaranteed that talks are under way to find fairer tariffs; said that Mozambique will not give up the survival of what he called the "goose that lays the golden eggs." "Mozal is proposing its tariffs and the Government, through the state-owned company HCB, which supplies, sells and exports electricity to Escom - this needs to be made clear - is at this moment discussing the tariffs, because on the basis of the tariffs that Mozal is proposing at the moment, if those tariffs were accepted, HCB could collapse," said the President. "What we are doing at this moment is defending the national interest and the interests of the Mozambican people. We have an added responsibility as a government; we cannot accept tariffs that will lead HCB to subsidise Mozal and cause HCB to collapse. So the talks continue and if we reach a consensus on the tariffs there is no problem," he declared.

a2379.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2379.speech: On the 45th SADC Summit: "The other positive aspect emerging from this summit was the adoption of the budget that will allow the full operationalisation of the Humanitarian Emergency Operations Centre based in Nacala, in the Republic of Mozambique, specifically in Nampula province, at a time when member states face countless financial difficulties. It is a budget that we think will be important, around 3.5 million dollars, which will help us maintain the work at the level of Nacala and also of the region (...)," he shared.

a2431.speaker: Tina Salam, Presidential spokesperson (DR Congo)
a2431.speech: Said President Felix Tshisekedi issued the commutation on Tuesday, downgrading the death sentences of three United States citizens convicted for taking part in a failed coup attempt last year to life imprisonment, six months after the US nationals – along with 34 others – were sentenced to death on charges of “terrorism” and “criminal association.”

a2431.speaker: Congolese army
a2431.speech: Said Christian Malanga was fatally shot while resisting arrest soon after livestreaming the attack on his social media.

a2431.speaker: Marcel Malanga, convicted US citizen and son of Christian Malanga
a2431.speech: Told the court that his father had forced him and Thompson to take part in the attack: “Dad had threatened to kill us if we did not follow his orders.”

a2431.speaker: US State Department
a2431.speech: Announced on Tuesday that President Donald Trump’s new senior adviser for Africa, Massad Boulos, will travel to DRC early this month to advance efforts for sustainable peace in eastern DRC and boost private sector investment.

a2519.speaker: Salim Valá, Mozambican Minister of Planning and Development
a2519.speech: says that funding cuts being implemented by the US government could affect some projects in Mozambique, highlighting the infrastructure implementation project in Zambézia financed under the Millennium Challenge Account as one of those that could be compromised, and hopes that the US government will yet reflect on this matter internally ; “The US is an important partner for Mozambique. We hope that this will be a period of internal reflection and I think that they will then review it. For example, we have the case of the province of Zambézia, which benefited from over US$500 million from the Millennium Challenge Account, and this could be very important for the economic and social transformation of the province of Zambézia. We believe that they will resume cooperation. The United States is an important partner, they need time to reflect internally to make adjustments to their strategies, taking into account that it is a new cycle.”

a2583.speaker: Reports from the news media, including official documentation of the US government
a2583.speech: have given credit to Biden for taking some of the most decisive actions for climate resilience, believed to have been a continuity from where Obama stopped.

a2583.speaker: Research results
a2583.speech: have shown that semiconductors are essential to climate-friendly energy alternatives such as renewable energy sources and electric cars.

a2583.speaker: Calculations (IRA emissions projections)
a2583.speech: show that if the IRA alone decreases emissions by 32-42%, the US may get much closer to its climate target by 2030.

a2583.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a2583.speech: has promised to carry out his aggressive deregulation policies, which include mandating that several existing regulations be repealed for each new one proposed. He has also declared his intention to "stop the flow of American tax dollars that are subsidizing Chinese electric vehicle battery companies" and to revoke the regulations implemented to promote EV adoption during the Biden administration. Additionally, he has declared his intention to ban investments in environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors.

a2583.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a2583.speech: has called climate change a "hoax" and pledged to withdraw the US from the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement again; has made very assertive statements about repealing the climate policies put in place by Joe Biden.

a2583.speaker: Alamu Ibrahim, strategic communication and digital marketing professional (author)
a2583.speech: argues that the Trump administration should not simply set out to abolish all that Biden had erected as climate protection frameworks, but should seek out the ambitious yet unrealistic climate commitments and find a way to modify the involvement of the United States in climate financing; he should prioritize bi-partisan climate-friendly policies, with emphasis on clean energy development, and continuing incentives, like those contained in the Inflation Reduction Act, and ensure the US remains a global leader in climate change mitigation.

a2642.speaker: International Committee of the Red Cross and the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (report)
a2642.speech: Report that there are 120 ongoing conflicts and 310 million people in need of humanitarian assistance around the world.

a2851.speaker: Clovis Ouedraogo and Ibrahim Gansore, Burkinabè living in the United States
a2851.speech: “We cannot remain spectators. Everyone can act in their own way,” they said, underlining their determination to take part in the patriotic battle being waged by Faso Mêbo.

a2851.speaker: Nilsun (agri-food company), represented by Ms Komi Farida
a2851.speech: Places this action within the framework of its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), thereby affirming its commitment to social and community causes.

a2859.speaker: Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemetti), leader of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a2859.speech: Accused Egypt of providing military support to Sudan’s Armed Forces (SAF).

a2859.speaker: Badr Abdelatty, Egypt’s Foreign Minister
a2859.speech: In an interview broadcast on Thursday, dismissed the RSF’s claims as “false and inflammatory,” reiterating Egypt’s stance of neutrality and emphasising Egypt’s ongoing efforts to mediate between Sudan’s warring factions ; “The security of Egypt is inseparably linked to that of Sudan. We reject any lies or exaggerations designed to involve Egypt in this conflict. Our focus remains on peace, not war” ; “Egypt will not be drawn into a war. Our priority is ensuring peace and security in the region, not fueling further conflict.”

a2859.speaker: Egyptian Foreign Ministry (statement)
a2859.speech: Issued a statement refuting the claims and warning that such rhetoric could derail peace efforts in the region: “Egypt is committed to supporting the Sudanese people through humanitarian efforts and diplomacy, not military intervention.”

a2859.speaker: Badr Abdelatty, Egypt’s Foreign Minister
a2859.speech: Emphasized Egypt’s ongoing role in hosting more than one million Sudanese refugees and its commitment to peaceful mediation.

a2859.speaker: RSF commanders
a2859.speech: Vowed to target Egypt’s Aswan High Dam, a critical infrastructure point on the Nile.

a2859.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a2859.speech: Announced a ban on Sudanese exports to Egypt, cutting off a key trade route for agricultural goods and livestock that pass through RSF-controlled regions like Darfur and Kordofan.

a2859.speaker: Rasha Awad, Sudanese civil activist
a2859.speech: “This is a clear provocation. It could trigger a dangerous confrontation between the RSF and Egypt.”

a2903.speaker: Investigating Directorate (ID) (statement)
a2903.speech: Says the summary acquittal of all the accused in its first-ever state capture trial - the R24.9 million Nulane fraud and money-laundering case - amounts to a "miscarriage of justice" that must be appealed; in a statement on Tuesday, the ID said that it would seek to appeal the decision on 10 different grounds; the ID denied that it had failed to present prima facie evidence that would require an answer from the accused. It said in the statement: "There are reasonable prospects that another court would come to a different conclusion and/or find that granting the discharge was a misdirection which was contrary to legal precedent, constituted a gross irregularity in the trial and was prejudicial to the State." ; The ID says that judgment was wrong and says there are "reasonable prospects that another court would find that the learned judge erred by making contradictory rulings which prejudiced the State when dealing with the issue of the admissibility of documentary evidence"; its statement further reads: "There are reasonable prospects that another court would find that the evidence presented before the court by the State called for a reply and that the accused ought to have been called upon to discharge their evidential burden."

a2903.speaker: Dubai Appeal Court (ruling)
a2903.speech: Refused to extradite Atul and Rajesh Gupta from the UAE.

a2903.speaker: Acting Judge Nompumelelo Gusha, Free State High Court
a2903.speech: Made the decision to discharge all of the accused without requiring them to defend themselves; when Gusha ruled that the State had failed to produce enough evidence to show the Gupta network was implicated in money laundering, she said she knew her decision would "invoke a sense of loss, if not dejection, to the citizenry of this country"; Gusha added that the State's financial expert witnesses in the case had sounded the "death knell" for its case; the judge further slammed the police's failed attempts to properly secure documents relevant to the Nulane trial as a "comedy of errors" and lambasted the State for "the lackadaisical manner in which this case was investigated and approached". "I can, therefore, not take this aspect any further than I have to save to conclude with the following African proverb: 'Haste and hurry can only bear children with many regrets along the way,'" she said.

a2903.speaker: The State (prosecution case)
a2903.speech: It was the State's case that the Free State Department of Agriculture paid R24.9 million to Nulane Investment, a company owned and controlled by former Transnet Board member Iqbal Sharma, for a fraudulent feasibility study for the Free State's flagship Mohoma Mobung project between 2011 and 2012; the State alleged that the Gupta family network, including its associate, Ronica Ragavan, and Islandsite Investments, was then involved in the subsequent laundering of the Nulane scam proceeds.

a2903.speaker: State's financial expert witnesses
a2903.speech: Admitted that they had made mistakes in their assessment of the Gupta network's finances and conceded that there was nothing untoward about its money transfers.

a2949.speaker: Neville Andre, Erongo governor
a2949.speech: Has called for urgent interventions as water shortages in the region have reached a critical level, with the situation now threatening livelihoods. "Water scarcity remains one of our most urgent challenges. While efforts have been made, the need to accelerate access to water cannot be overstated," Andre stated. ; Said the Erongo Water Crisis Committee was established to address the region's water issues, and identified several challenges, including water losses due to leakages, vandalism of infrastructure and illegal water connections.

a2949.speaker: Neville Andre, Erongo governor
a2949.speech: Expressed concern during the agriculture ministry's quarterly review workshop in Swakopmund: "Our region continues to suffer from one of the most devastating droughts in recent years. The prolonged dry spells have significantly impacted farmers, rural communities and livestock." ; Noted that a key concern is the slow response of the Rural Water Supply office in addressing critical shortages: "Delays in intervention have left many communities struggling to access this essential resource. Our farmers, the backbone of food production and economic sustainability, require timely support and incentives to cope with these conditions." ; Urged immediate measures to strengthen the Rural Water Supply office, whether through increased funding, additional personnel or improved logistical support, saying a well-equipped and responsive office is essential to prevent prolonged hardships. ; Acknowledged the ministry's support in the installation of the Ozondati pipeline, in supplying water to remote areas, and progress towards constructing a second desalination plant: "These are achievements to be proud of, and we appreciate your leadership."

a2949.speaker: Calle Schlettwein, Namibian agriculture minister
a2949.speech: Acknowledged the country's ongoing water crisis. "The President declared a drought emergency at the start of the financial year. Yet, rainfall distribution has been uneven, with some areas still facing severe drought conditions. The public expects us to continue mitigating the impacts of drought, both nationally and at the household level," he said. ; Said his ministry is fast-tracking drought relief measures: "We should expedite the implementation of the measures in place to achieve immediate impact on the ground." ; Said the ministry has prioritised several interventions, including the construction of 16 earth dams, the drilling of 136 boreholes, and the installation of 238 sanitation facilities in rural areas: "These measures are designed to alleviate the immediate impacts of drought and safeguard livelihoods," calling on stakeholders to enhance their efforts. ; Highlighted that agriculture remains the backbone of rural communities, and underscored the importance of water and land reform in ensuring food security, economic prosperity and social equity; called for a renewed focus on small-scale and resettlement farmers, as well as livestock production and veterinary services.

a2949.speaker: Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila, Prime Minister of Namibia
a2949.speech: Revealed late last year, addressing the 9th Session of the Africa Regional Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction Conference in late October 2024, that Namibia faces a funding shortfall of about N$482 million to shield 1.26 million drought-stricken citizens from a looming hunger crisis, from the planned N$1.6 billion drought relief programme. "Therefore, the government is appealing for assistance. Positive responses to our appeal for assistance have been received from development partners, for which we are grateful. Assistance comes in the form of cash and in-kind donations of food and equipment made directly to the government, and donations in cash and kind made through UN agencies. The Southern African Development Community (SADC) region is currently going through one of the worst droughts in recent years, induced by the El Nino phenomenon."

a2949.speaker: President Nangolo Mbumba of Namibia
a2949.speech: Last May declared a state of emergency on the protracted drought, which has seen the country's aggregated cereal production of white maize, sorghum, pearl millet and wheat decreasing by 53%, while dam levels countrywide had dropped by 69.7%.

a2949.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, July/September 2024 report
a2949.speech: Stated that about 1.15 million people, which is 38% of the country's population, were classified in Phase 3 (Crisis) or above, necessitating urgent humanitarian assistance to mitigate food consumption gaps and protect livelihoods.

a2973.speaker: Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC) (report, “The Role of GNPC in the upstream petroleum industry: challenges and Prospects”)
a2973.speech: Has cautioned that the survival of the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) risks collapsing as the government’s indebtedness to the corporation continues to pile up; according to PIAC, as of the end of 2022, the government owes the GNPC to the tune of $1.14 billion, an amount which it said represents payments made on behalf of the government and SOEs, national and local projects plus gas supplied to the Ghana National Gas Company (GNGC) ; “GNPC risks collapse after 2026 when it ceases to receive funding from the Petroleum Holding Fund” ; “The PRMA mentions that the NOC is to be funded for 15 years following the start of commercial production of crude oil, following which it will no longer be supported with funds from the PHF. This means that after 2026, GNPC will no longer receive funding from the PHF. Given the challenges that confront the Corporation, it may not be able to survive without government support if the enactment is implemented.”

a2973.speaker: Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC)
a2973.speech: Again raises red flags about the corporation’s expenditures, which fall outside its core mandate and are constraining its ability to operate as a standalone commercial entity in the petroleum industry; for example, as of the end of 2022, total expenditure on the various Gas Enclave roads in the Western region stood at US$124.66 million; these expenditures, according to PIAC, often made on behalf of the government and other agencies, are undermining GNPC’s capacity to fulfil its primary responsibilities and contribute to its development ; Also fears that the Corporation is subject to political capture, which often compels it to undertake quasi-fiscal expenditures and advances to other parastatals which ordinarily should be the preserve of the central government.

a2973.speaker: Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC) (recommendations)
a2973.speech: Recommends several measures to address these challenges and ensure the sustainability of GNPC: firstly, PIAC wants GNPC to commit more funds to its mandate and development by desisting from making payments in favour of the government and its agencies whilst calling for urgent action to retrieve funds owed to the Corporation; it also called on management of GNPC to desist from the practice where some agencies approach it to fund their programmes and projects.

a3004.speaker: World Bank (July 2025 Malawi Economic Monitor)
a3004.speech: Says despite employing some emergency measures, a long-term solution to address structural foreign exchange market challenges is yet to be implemented; acknowledged that the country is still facing challenges in bolstering foreign exchange reserves and narrowing the spread between the official and parallel market rates ; "Reserve Bank of Malawi [RBM] has announced a reduction in the mandatory conversion rate for export revenues from 30 percent to 25 percent, with further reductions for qualifying companies anticipated. However, the disappointing tobacco and macadamia harvests have neither significantly bolstered foreign exchange reserves, nor reduced the exchange rate differential between the official and the parallel market."

a3004.speaker: World Bank data
a3004.speech: Shows the spread between bureau rate and official rate is sitting at about 10 to 12 percent while the gap between the parallel market and official rates has widened, reportedly peaking at over 150 percent in early 2025.

a3004.speaker: Joseph Mwanamvekha, former Finance minister of Malawi
a3004.speech: Said in an interview that while the policy change could help to improve foreign exchange reserves and curb the black market, without forex in the banks, it will not work.

a3004.speaker: Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) data
a3004.speech: Shows that the economy's total reserves position declined to $569.5 million or an equivalent of 2.3 months of imports cover in February 2025 compared to $570.6 million or 2.31 months of imports in the preceding month.

a3004.speaker: Malawi Confederation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry (2025 First Quarter Business Review)
a3004.speech: Observed that the dip in reserves, especially due to a decline in private sector foreign exchange holdings, could signal tightening access to foreign exchange availability for businesses ; "Companies that import essential inputs may face longer delays in obtaining foreign currency, disrupting production timelines, especially in manufacturing, agro-processing and retail sectors."

a3004.speaker: Kisu Simwaka, RBM Deputy Governor responsible for economics and regulation (Facebook post)
a3004.speech: Conceded in his Facebook post recently that the country's export receipts only pay for one-third of the import bill, leaving the country to increasingly rely on foreign aid flows, external borrowing and financial derivatives such as foreign currency swaps to pay for the remaining two-thirds of the import bill.

a3163.speaker: Three Nigerian financial powers, among them Aliko Dangote, businessmen
a3163.speech: have promised the trifling sum of 80 million CFA francs to each player of the Nigerian team should it qualify for the next World Cup.

a3163.speaker: Gernot Rohr, national coach of Benin
a3163.speech: At the pre-match press conference: "We arrive here with our destiny in our own hands. If we win, we are qualified. If we draw, it will depend on the result of the other match between South Africa and Rwanda. But we don't want to calculate too much. We are going to concentrate on our match. It will be difficult, but for us it is always possible to win in Nigeria. I think we took a first step by beating the Super Eagles in the first leg, in Abidjan. There now remains a second step: to beat them here. It will be very difficult, of course. But as you know, for two and a half years we have played all our matches in Abidjan, far from Benin. My team has become mentally strong. It is not afraid to face a team like the Super Eagles away from home. We have good hope."

a3163.speaker: Gernot Rohr, national coach of Benin and former coach of Nigeria's Super Eagles
a3163.speech: let it be known this Monday 13 October 2025 before the media that only the objective of allowing Benin to write a fine page of its history guides his steps: "Here, there is no emotion, there is professionalism. They are good memories, certainly, but we are in another context. There is no place for emotion. We are happy to see familiar faces again, but we are here to do our job. We have one step left to take to qualify for this World Cup. Now that we are so close, we want to do it. So, emotion: NO! Concentration: YES! And above all COMBATIVENESS. And that, I know my team is capable of fighting together, like real Cheetahs."

a3190.speaker: Tabitha Chawinga, Malawi women's football superstar
a3190.speech: Has confirmed her return to the Scorchers after almost two years for the Cosafa Women's Championship in Gqeberha, South Africa, from October 22 to November 2.

a3190.speaker: Gomezgani Zakazaka, Football Association of Malawi competitions and communications director
a3190.speech: Confirmed in an interview that Tabitha, who has in the past been called into Scorchers squad but never made it due to club commitments, will captain the side in South Africa ; “It's confirmed. Tabitha will be available for the Cosafa Women's Championship. But she will not finish the tournament as she has to return after Fifa window.”

a3190.speaker: Gomezgani Zakazaka, Football Association of Malawi competitions and communications director
a3190.speech: Said Thom, Madise, Chikupila, Mkandawire and Khumalo also confirmed their availability while Temwa, Kabzere and Chavinda are yet to do so.

a3190.speaker: Lovemore Fazili, Scorchers coach
a3190.speech: Says camping for local players started well on Saturday at Mpira Village in Chiwembe, Blantyre ; “We started camp on Saturday with the medical check-ups and the other medical issues. Then on Sunday we were on the ground. Our main focus is on the local players since we only have them at the moment.”

a3308.speaker: Gerson Msigwa, Government Spokesperson (Tanzania)
a3308.speech: Said that after the suspension of assistance from the United States was announced, some people who use antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) went to health facilities and asked to be given two to three years' worth of medicines, arising from the fear that had built up among them about what would happen once the medicines they use stopped being brought in.

a3308.speaker: Gerson Msigwa, Government Spokesperson (Tanzania)
a3308.speech: Reassured people living with HIV about the availability of medicines, saying the Government has prepared itself sufficiently so that if stakeholders' funds are cut off, those medicines will be bought and distributed to those concerned: "The ARVs are there. Tanzanians who use the medicines, live in peace, get on with your work and continue to take precautions against infecting others. The medicines are there, your Government is there, it will look after you and we will not run out and you will not go without medicines." ; "Now if you take those medicines and go and keep them at home they will spoil, and if they spoil they will not help you, they will bring you health problems. Let them stay at the facilities where they are well stored, and you should follow the arrangement you are given by the specialists to go and collect medicines as you have been scheduled." ; "You are safe, get on with your work, let us continue to implement all the interventions to combat HIV infection. I ask my fellow young people to take precautions - AIDS is still here, let us protect ourselves so that we can end it; today's world is talking about ending AIDS and let us Tanzanians be the first."

a3308.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a3308.speech: On January 28 this year, ordered a halt to the supply of medicines for AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis to countries that receive assistance from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).

a3308.speaker: International circles/reports
a3308.speech: According to international circles, that order is expected to affect millions of people who depend on treatment services through programmes such as the United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR).

a3308.speaker: Aid organisations, including Chemonics
a3308.speech: Have said that the step will disrupt the availability of medicines and services for the people who are most at risk.

a3361.speaker: Gideon Enoch Abbequaye, Registrar of the University of Cape Coast and Secretary to the university's Governing Council (letter)
a3361.speech: A letter signed by him stated that Prof Aheto was appointed as Pro-Vice-Chancellor at a special meeting on December 19, 2024.

a3459.speaker: Mark Harrington, co-founder of the Treatment Action Group
a3459.speech: Rallied the crowd of about 400 in Yerba Buena Gardens: "Research is under attack! What do we do?" ; "People with Aids are under attack. What do we do" ; "Let me remind you, in the early years people with HIV had to fight for the right to be studied" ; "What the people in the White House are now [again] doing is an act of premeditated murder on 40-million people living with HIV around the world" ; "When they say what we can and can't study, they're imposing fascist restraints on the kind of science that we need to end this pandemic" ; "They say sex and gender are the same thing. But that's such bullshit. It flies in the face of so much science."

a3459.speaker: Mitchell Warren, New York-based advocacy organisation Avac
a3459.speech: Explained how researchers are self-censoring their presentations: "What you found in some cases, was someone presenting a study about men who have sex with men, that would have included, for example, people who are transgender. Sixty-one days [before] you might have seen this study focused on gay men, other men who have sex with men, transgender women and men and non-binary individuals. But now you'd see it saying, this is for sexually active people or men who have sex with men. People are very guarded right now."

a3459.speaker: Mitchell Warren, New York-based advocacy organisation Avac
a3459.speech: Said the most common question from attendees this year was: "I'm a 30-year-old postdoctoral student and thinking about a career in HIV. Do I have a future?" ; cautioned: "If a young researcher is wondering if they have a future in HIV research, and don't join this field because of that, in 10, 20, 30 years they're not going to have created the next big discoveries. You have to create a constant cycle of new ideas, new investigators, new advocates, and that's also being disrupted here."

a3459.speaker: Chris Beyrer, epidemiologist and director of the Duke Global Health Institute
a3459.speech: In his plenary: "I want to start with a few words that define the HIV response and our field. Diversity. Equity. Inclusion" ; "Diversity is in our DNA. It's who we are. We can't not address diversity, because we're dealing with a diverse HIV pandemic. And the fact that three quarters of all people living with HIV on this planet access antiretroviral therapy, is the greatest achievement of equity in global health. We're not going to give it up" ; told Bhekisisa after his plenary: "The reality is that you can't pick and choose which kinds of populations you care about and which you don't in a pandemic. You have to deal with everybody who's affected... whatever you think about transgender women, the fact is that they're among the groups that have the highest risk and the highest prevalence for HIV. So, they have to be part of service provision."

a3459.speaker: Chris Beyrer, epidemiologist and director of the Duke Global Health Institute
a3459.speech: Explained that the consequences of research funding cuts have already been felt and many studies are on pause; said "One of the reasons South Africa has done so well with HIV research is because of the extraordinary depth of scientific talent. Now we're worried about our international partnerships for collaborative research with countries like South Africa, and also China"; said HIV prevention research is unlikely to be funded by the US government in future, but that he has faith in court proceedings taking their course: "I lost my first partner to Aids in 1991 when I was just finishing my medical training. Of a whole circle of guys in New York who were our friends, there are only two of us who survived. I've held on to those men and those losses my whole life. I've never given up, and I'm not going to now."

a3459.speaker: Franco Chevalier, internal medicine doctor and infectious diseases fellow at the University of California San Francisco
a3459.speech: Told the rally: "As an immigrant, I had to navigate a system that wasn't always designed for people who looked like me and who had to endure the things I had to as a gay Afro Latino. But I found mentors, scientists who believed in me" ; warned: "None of this would have been possible without the investment of the US government in research. Without proper funding we not only risk losing the entire next generation of scientists, which the cuts will disproportionately impact, but we run the danger of losing the resources that have kept millions alive and have prevented countless people from becoming infected in the first place."

a3459.speaker: Delegates at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (Croi)
a3459.speech: Say some US government-funded presentations were retracted, others were redacted, had their titles changed, or the names of government authors removed, to adhere to the new doublespeak of the Trump era.

a3459.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (executive orders)
a3459.speech: Signed an executive order on the night of his inauguration, January 20, banning people's right to identify as transgender or non-binary individuals, declaring there are only two genders: male and female; signed an executive order in January to end all diversity, equity and inclusion programmes; and signed an additional executive order banning all foreign aid to South Africa, which includes money used for research projects.

a3459.speaker: Science magazine
a3459.speech: Reports health researchers who work in South Africa are on red alert after hearing the NIH could terminate all grants that fund work in the country; reports that a March 12 email on behalf of the NIH's acting director, Matthew Memoli, asked researchers at the NIH to compile lists of South Africa-related grants — "The email instructed NIH's institutes and centres to 'please provide any information related to NIH investment in South Africa to [NIH's executive secretary] by 5pm'" — and that "Similar wording accompanied earlier NIH requests for information that led to the termination of dozens of grants involving transgender health, vaccine hesitancy, and other topics the administration does not support".

a3459.speaker: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (list of grants)
a3459.speech: Compiled a list naming 237 grants, most involving HIV or tuberculosis research.

a3459.speaker: Many organisations funded through the CDC in South Africa
a3459.speech: Say they have only received budgets until the end of September.

a3488.speaker: Lucy Tamlyn, U.S. Ambassador to Benin
a3488.speech: In her message, told participants that over the three days they would learn that these principles of American law govern her own conduct and that of the embassy's employees, because as a federal government employee she is subject to an essential public service obligation stipulating that all employees "must report waste, fraud, abuse and corruption to the competent authorities" ; for that reason she invited everyone to take part in the efforts to fight corruption, in order to guarantee the proper execution of the MCA programme and open the way to a better future for Benin.

a3488.speaker: Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Minister of State for Planning and Development of Benin
a3488.speech: Officially launching the workshop, recalled that the fight against corruption and impunity are key eligibility criteria for MCA programmes; that in 2013 Benin's eligibility for MCC resources was suspended because of unsatisfactory results in this area; and that as the second Compact is now being implemented it is imperative to maintain permanent vigilance in order to sustain and improve progress on this indicator.

a3488.speaker: Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Minister of State for Planning and Development of Benin
a3488.speech: "My presence here at your side therefore has a double meaning. First, it is a matter of associating myself with an initiative whose spirit and letter are in line with the Government's commitments. Second, as you know, I have taken some interest in corruption in the past. As a result, I have come to the conclusion that in order to fight corruption effectively, one must among other things change people's attitude towards the phenomenon" ; reiterated his full satisfaction with this Millennium Challenge Corporation training and called for it to be held regularly.

a3676.speaker: Bola Tinubu, President of Nigeria
a3676.speech: Directed the compulsory implementation of health insurance across all Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) in line with the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) Act, 2022; instructed the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, George Akume, to release a service-wide circular mandating compliance.

a3676.speaker: Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy (statement)
a3676.speech: Announced the directive in a statement issued on Wednesday: “Where desired, MDAs may take up supplementary private insurance coverage in accordance with the NHIA Act”; “All entities participating in public procurement must present a valid NHIA-issued Health Insurance Certificate as part of their eligibility documentation”; “This certificate confirms compliance with the mandatory health insurance requirement and serves as a condition precedent for continuing any procurement-related engagement.”

a3676.speaker: Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy
a3676.speech: Explained that the directive is aimed at expanding health coverage, safeguarding workers, reducing out-of-pocket expenditures and promoting accountability in both the public and private sectors; noted that although the NHIA Act of 2022 mandates compulsory health insurance for all Nigerians, coverage remains low three years after its passage.

a3676.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a3676.speech: Announced on Monday, at the opening of a four-day National Health Financing Policy Dialogue in Abuja, that Nigeria aims to enrol at least 44 million citizens into the National Health Insurance Scheme by 2030.

a3676.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a3676.speech: Emphasised the urgency of reforming health financing in Nigeria; said the federal government has consistently funded the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) and introduced emergency allocations to cushion the suspension of foreign aid; added that the ministry is considering legislation to double BHCPF funding from one to two per cent of consolidated revenue, alongside efforts to enrol 44 million Nigerians into the National Health Insurance scheme by 2030.

a3676.speaker: The presidency
a3676.speech: According to the presidency, the new directive covers five key areas, including the compulsory enrolment of all MDA employees under the NHIA health insurance plan; applicants seeking licences, permits, or other official approvals from MDAs must present valid NHIA Health Insurance Certificates before issuance or renewal; the NHIA will establish a digital platform to enable real-time verification of health insurance certificates and improve transparency; and MDAs are required to set up internal procedures for verifying certificates and monitoring compliance in collaboration with the NHIA.

a3804.speaker: Martin Mpata, general manager of Mapeto DWSM Limited
a3804.speech: Said the firm, which requires about 24 million tonnes of cotton to sustainably run its processing plant, only secures up to 6 million kg ; "If we can have adequate supplies of cotton, we should be able to employ 42 percent more than what we are currently employing (2,800 workers)."

a3804.speaker: Jacob Nyirongo, Chief Executive Officer, Farmers Union of Malawi
a3804.speech: Called on the government to follow through on the promise of revitalising the cotton industry by investing in systems that enable farmers to profitably produce cotton.

a3804.speaker: International cotton conference of eastern and southern African countries (participants)
a3804.speech: It emerged from the conference that the region faces similar challenges, and that cotton seed is not adequately supplied at this point in time, which is already affecting planning by farmers.

a3804.speaker: Cosmas Luwanda, Executive Secretary, Cotton Council of Malawi
a3804.speech: Said a structured cotton market is being put in place to sanitise the industry following the establishment of the council.

a3970.speaker: STV (independent television station report)
a3970.speech: Reported that the system will ensure access to clean drinking water for over 8,000 people.

a3970.speaker: Filipe Nyusi, Mozambican President
a3970.speech: Downplayed the repeated and scornful criticism by his detractors of the inaugurations he has been commissioning: “From what we heard, the new system will bring drinking water to 8,000 consumers. It is a motive for great pride for us, but for others it is just a small system which does not deserve the president’s attention” ; pointed out that his critics seem to have forgotten that there are a great many small systems scattered across the country within the communities, villages and towns where large numbers of Mozambicans live.

a3970.speaker: Filipe Nyusi, Mozambican President
a3970.speech: Said there have been enormous improvements in access to water over the past decade: “From 2015 to the present, the proportion of the rural Mozambican population with access to safe drinking water has risen from 38.9 per cent to 56 per cent” ; said access to clean water was no longer a privilege of people living in the major urban centres and that, including both urban and rural areas, the number of people with access to safe water has risen to 65 per cent, about 20 million Mozambicans.

a3970.speaker: David Young, Deputy Director of the USAID office in Mozambique (speaking on behalf of the country’s cooperation partners)
a3970.speech: Said the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom will continue to work in close partnership with the Mozambican government to provide more water and improve sanitation: “For the country’s water and sanitation programme, the US Government, through its development agency USAID, is channeling 20 million dollars for improved access to drinking water and sanitation for over one million people in Mozambique”.

a3970.speaker: Representative of the local community of Pussulane
a3970.speech: “The newly inaugurated water supply system will have a great impact on our lives, since the long distances we used to walk to fetch water have now been reduced”.

a3976.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, Deputy Special Representative and Humanitarian Coordinator for the DRC
a3976.speech: Updated journalists on latest developments and obstacles to aid delivery; said the situation in the east remains extremely volatile, with escalating armed clashes, mass displacement and increasing insecurity in both North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. “But there are more than the M23 in the DRC.
