For example, this morning we learned that at least 52 civilians were reportedly killed in Ituri by the armed group called CODECO.” ; said the M23 and Rwandan forces are advancing towards the Kavumu Airport, and warned: “Clashes are ongoing, including today, and they’re likely to continue, and the M23 may use alternative routes to progress towards the town of Bukavu in the coming days, with again massive consequences on the civilian population.”

a3976.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, Deputy Special Representative and Humanitarian Coordinator for the DRC
a3976.speech: Said the past few days have seen “recourse to mob justice in a context of proliferation of light weapons and ammunition, and the looting of court houses”, presenting a further challenge to “reinstating the rule of law in a zone with a tragic legacy of gross humanitarian gross human rights violations and impunity” ; “Furthermore, several human rights defenders, in particular those working on issues of sexual and gender-based violence, as well as journalists, report persistent threats and incidents of forced disappearance and summary execution targeting them.”

a3976.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, Deputy Special Representative and Humanitarian Coordinator for the DRC
a3976.speech: Noted that things have improved slightly as efforts are underway to restore electricity and re-establish the water supply, that school activities have partially resumed and that public services remain partially functional in Goma, but that hospitals are still overwhelmed: “Mortuaries are saturated, and medical teams have to cope with an unprecedented number of war wounded, with a shortage of medicine and medical supplies” ; “Risks of epidemics are high in the city, in particular cholera and mpox. Food prices have risen, and more and more people need food assistance every day.”

a3976.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, Deputy Special Representative and Humanitarian Coordinator for the DRC
a3976.speech: Said humanitarian partners remain on the ground working to prevent and alleviate suffering and are moving to strengthen response now that the situation has stabilized; said many facilities belonging to the UN and international aid agencies were looted during the height of the fighting in Goma and millions of dollars in supplies were lost; said getting aid to Goma is another major obstacle as the airport remains closed: “Without this airport we cannot evacuate the seriously injured, transport the necessary medical supplies or bring in humanitarian reinforcement. All parties must act now to work together to re-open the airport and allow humanitarian flights to resume.”

a3976.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, Deputy Special Representative and Humanitarian Coordinator for the DRC
a3976.speech: On the Trump administration’s decision to temporarily suspend foreign aid: “This is a major source of concern with several UN agencies and international NGOs active on the ground having seen their operations at best severely impact, if not halted” ; “Our humanitarian response is the most dependent in the world on US assistance. We were 70 per cent funded by US funding, so this is having major impact.” In response to a journalist’s question, explained that humanitarians required $2.5 billion for their operations in 2024 and garnered $1.3 billion – the highest amount ever received in the DRC for humanitarian response – of which $910 million came from the US alone: “The ultra-dependence on US funding means a lot of programmes had to shut down on everything we are doing. So, it’s emergency health, it’s emergency shelter…it’s coordination capacity” ; “The only exception so far, but we hope there will be more exceptions, was emergency food assistance.”

a3976.speaker: Bruno Lemarquis, Deputy Special Representative and Humanitarian Coordinator for the DRC
a3976.speech: “Despite these challenges, we aim to stay and deliver”; on behalf of the humanitarian community, reiterated the call for “all the parties to end hostilities and to return to the political process” and urged the international community “to intensify its support for the humanitarian response in this complicated area.”

a4121.speaker: Mthuli Ncube, Zimbabwe Finance Minister
a4121.speech: Said Zimbabwe will have to rely on taxes to plug a large gap left by the US foreign aid cuts: “We are talking about US$200 million or so (on PEPFAR) that is at stake. Our response really should be domestic resource mobilisation, which is what we have been doing” ; said the tax on sugar content in drinks, plus a one percent tax recently introduced on fast food, would play a crucial role in the domestic resource mobilisation drive, and added that Zimbabweans already pay an AIDS levy and sin taxes on beer, also targeted at healthcare ; “All these taxes form the base that we can use to build resource mobilisation to support our health needs. It has to be through this kind of thinking where we raise resources to support the health sector domestically as foreign funding is under threat.”

a4121.speaker: FBC Securities
a4121.speech: Said enhancing domestic resource mobilisation can mitigate the challenges, although the efficiency of such strategies might be limited given that the economy is already overtaxed and highly informal: “To mitigate these challenges, the Zimbabwean government must take decisive action by strengthening domestic revenue mobilization, restoring investor confidence, restructuring state-owned enterprises, and improving governance and fiscal discipline.”

a4121.speaker: Tendai Westerhoff, National Director of the Pan-African Positive Women’s Coalition
a4121.speech: Emphasised the need to prioritise sustainability, explaining that the problem with donor funding is its unpredictability: “We should form resilient systems in terms of ensuring that we have domestic resourcing so that if donors pull out, we can continue with programs because pulling out of donors does not hold HIV infections. We are still getting new HIV infections.”

a4121.speaker: Tendai Westerhoff, National Director of the Pan-African Positive Women’s Coalition
a4121.speech: Called on countries to commit to the 15 percent of the Abuja Declaration, which is not happening in most cases: “A lot of countries, including us, we are still falling far short of that 15 percent commitment to the health budget, so that we can strengthen the capacity at every level to fight HIV and AIDS.”

a4121.speaker: Martha Tholanah, antiretroviral patient at Parirenyatwa Hospital
a4121.speech: Expressed concern regarding Zimbabwe’s capacity to fill the gap left by PEPFAR: “The funding has been assisting in terms of treatment, prevention care and livelihoods. As you know, there is no health without livelihoods. Now, how do we start building from the rug that has suddenly been pulled from under our feet?” ; “This means our reliance on foreign funding is too heavy. We need more domestic resources for health from the national treasury. Partners should complement the government, not the other way round.”

a4127.speaker: Winston Chitando, Zimbabwe Mines Minister
a4127.speech: Said on Tuesday that Zimbabwe will ban the export of lithium concentrates from 2027 as it extends its push for more local processing; said lithium sulphate plants were currently being developed at two Zimbabwean mines, Bikita Minerals, owned by Sinomine, and Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe, owned by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt: “Because of that capacity which is now in the country, the export of all lithium concentrates will be banned from January 2027,” said during a media briefing following a weekly cabinet meeting.

a4142.speaker: Report of the Trade Committee of the Gambian Parliament
a4142.speech: Contains the development that Gambian authorities and their Senegalese counterparts have agreed to address issues affecting transit traders, such as the exorbitant and unnecessary charges and delays that traders from the two countries are faced with ; one of such issues highlighted in the report is the payment of exorbitant escort charges which traders are obliged to pay to avert unnecessary delay at borders ; according to the report, the National Assembly is responsible for performing oversight of the activities of the Trade Ministry and its satellite institutions or agencies.

a4142.speaker: Hon. Kebba Jallow, Chairperson of the Trade Committee of the Gambian Parliament
a4142.speech: “This mandate is vested on the committee by the National Assembly under Section 109 of the 1997 Constitution and Standing Order 97. In addition, the committee has the power under Section 109 subsection 2 (B), to investigate any matter of public interest,” he said, reminding his colleagues that during the Fifth Legislature, the committee embarked on a countrywide tour, to both official and unofficial border posts, to assess and generate firsthand information on the implementation of the ECOWAS Protocol and Conventions for the transit of goods across the country’s borders ; “In this regard, GRA officials informed the committee that their Senegalese counterparts do not implement the ECOWAS Inter State Road Transit Convention (ISRT)” ; he said the committee learned that transit goods from the Gambia are being charged prohibitive or double escort fees, to the extent of making “transit trade in the Gambia unattractive, which in turn affects custom revenue” ; “In the same vein, the Gambian traders in transit trade across the border expressed similar concern,” he said ; he said customs officials on the borders subject transit traders to unnecessary charges that contravene the provisions of the ISRT Convention “by imposing unnecessary and multiple escort fees, leaving the traders without choice but to pay, to avert unnecessary delay.” ; he said that after the meeting the authorities of the two states agreed to dedicate their efforts to engage all the relevant authorities in their respective countries on the matter; and to ensure that trade and other border-related issues are addressed ; “There is a need to interconnect the two countries’ customs IT systems (GAINDE and ASYCUDA) in order to harmonize procedures and thus solve the problem of transit documents. The committee also recommended that GRA through the relevant Ministry, engage ECOWAS to operationalize the Interconnected System for the Management of Goods in Transit (SIGMAT) between the two countries,” he said.

a4142.speaker: GRA (Gambia Revenue Authority) officials
a4142.speech: Informed the committee that their Senegalese counterparts do not implement the ECOWAS Inter State Road Transit Convention (ISRT), and later informed the committee that the situation remains the same, “because their counterparts are not implementing this convention.”

a4142.speaker: Senegalese authorities (met during the visit)
a4142.speech: “The authorities emphasized the importance of the visit as the two states are inseparable and share the same people, culture, social values, and economic activities among others,” he said. He reiterated among others “that the bond between the Gambia and Senegal makes the countries as one, only to be divided by the West for their own interest.”

a4142.speaker: Gambian delegation / members of the Gambia’s Trade Committee
a4142.speech: Highlighted the need for collaboration between the two states, as they are all part of ECOWAS and subjected to the convention and protocols of the regional bloc ; “The Gambian delegation informed their Senegalese counterparts that the non-trade barriers that transit traders experience from one border to another is exorbitant and therefore there is a need for dialogue to address these challenges,” he said ; told their Senegalese counterparts that the proper implementation of the convention is beneficial to the two states and therefore the need for them to come together for the smooth implementation of the convention.

a4142.speaker: Gambian traders in transit trade
a4142.speech: Expressed similar concern about prohibitive or double escort fees charged across the border.

a4145.speaker: Brian Shukan, United States Ambassador to Benin
a4145.speech: Recalled that the partnership between his country and Benin is founded on shared values, notably a commitment to democracy, sustainable development, economic opportunity, security cooperation and strengthening ties between the two peoples. “We appreciate our productive partnership with the government of President Patrice Talon to develop economic opportunities and the well-being of all Beninese,” he affirmed. He cited as examples the achievements of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) since 2016, notably in access to land, justice and financial services, modernization of the port of Cotonou, access to energy and improvement of the Benin-Niger corridor whose compact was recently signed. He also recalled the achievements of the United States Agency for International Development in the fight against malaria and tropical diseases, and in improving maternal, neonatal and child health and family planning, as well as its work in water, sanitation and hygiene, good governance, human rights and social cohesion. He also mentioned the actions of Peace Corps volunteers in Benin over 55 years, those of the US African Development Foundation, cooperation with the Beninese security and defence forces, the ambassador’s special self-help fund, and US-sponsored professional and cultural exchange programmes.

a4145.speaker: Erick Jean-Marie Zinsou, Secretary General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Benin
a4145.speech: Supported the ambassador’s remarks by reviewing some of the achievements, actions and programmes of the United States in Benin, before expressing the gratitude of the Beninese executive to the American government and people. On the achievements of MCA-Benin II, he assured the American partner that arrangements have been made to ensure their sustainability. Concerning the regional compact, he recalled that the modalities for finalizing this new compact are being finalized in order ultimately to boost the Beninese economy.

a4159.speaker: ZOLA Electric and its partners
a4159.speech: Reaffirmed their commitment to supporting the government’s efforts in implementing the Dar es Salaam Declaration, a key initiative aimed at expanding clean cooking and electricity access while increasing the share of renewable energy in Africa’s energy mix.

a4159.speaker: Bill Lenihan, Chief Executive Officer of ZOLA Electric
a4159.speech: Stated at a press conference in Dar es Salaam that the company will contribute its expertise to accelerating decentralised renewable energy adoption, particularly in off-grid areas, which are critical to achieving universal energy access: “With over a decade of experience in delivering innovative energy solutions, our mission of ‘Energy Equality for All’ aligns seamlessly with the objectives of Mission 300.” ; “Our solutions are uniquely positioned to address Africa’s energy access challenges, including unreliable grid infrastructure and the need for scalable, cost-effective alternatives.” ; Described Mission 300 as a transformative opportunity to bridge Africa’s energy gap: “Our platform not only brings clean, reliable energy to underserved communities but also empowers local businesses to build sustainable energy enterprises. This is how we drive lasting impact at scale.”

a4168.speaker: Malawi Government
a4168.speech: Says it has mutually agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to suspend the four-year $175 million (about K306 billion) Extended Credit Facility (ECF).

a4168.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury (statement)
a4168.speech: Said in a statement that the decision to have the programme “lapsed” followed a mutual resolve between Malawi and the Bretton Woods institution ; “The programme faced a number of exogenous shocks which made it difficult for the supply side to assist both increased revenue and enhanced production. This resolution allows the political environment necessary for the progression of the ECF programme to normalise as is expected after the elections in September 2025, thus enabling government to leverage its fresh electoral mandate in negotiating a more sustainable Extended Credit Facility package for Malawi’s macroeconomic stability going forward.”

a4168.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury
a4168.speech: Said recognising the extent of the exogenous shocks that affected the country, the IMF has agreed to deploy a mission at the end of May 2025 to conduct a monitoring and consultation exercise for Malawi’s economic mainstays in preparation for “a tailor-made Malawi programme” in the future.

a4168.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF) update on Malawi’s ECF
a4168.speech: Said that while the ECF arrangement has expired, it was engaged in Article IV consultations with the Malawi Government ; “The IMF continues to work with the authorities in other ways within its mandate to support Malawi. This includes providing technical assistance to help modernise Malawi’s economic policies, strengthen its institutions and their capacity to implement reforms. In addition, a range of tailored financing tools is still available to give Malawi some breathing room to adjust policies in an orderly manner.” ; confirmed that in accordance with its financing policies for low-income countries, Malawi’s ECF automatically terminated as no review was completed over an 18-month period.

a4168.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a4168.speech: According to the IMF, one of the most urgent goals of the ECF was to support the authorities’ commitment to restore macroeconomic stability and creating an environment of low or moderate inflation as well as a stable exchange rate.

a4168.speaker: Capital Hill (Malawi Treasury/Government)
a4168.speech: Said the series of reforms Malawi had implemented were tough, but necessary to convince development partners that the government was committed to reforms to revitalise the ailing economy.

a4168.speaker: Joseph Mwanamvekha, former minister of Finance and opposition Democratic Progressive Party legislator
a4168.speech: Said the country risks losing the $140 million that was expected from the IMF and the $80 million from the World Bank which were largely dependent on the ECF programme ; said Malawi could also lose other budget-related support from other cooperating partners ; “What is more worrying is that this is happening against a backdrop of the recent loss of support from the United States of America Government through USAid. This is sad and unfortunate, though not surprising! We knew the ECF programme was off-track way back and that MCP [Malawi Congress Party] government has been missing all the agreed targets and benchmarks since its inception.”

a4168.speaker: Dalitso Kabambe, UTM Party president and former Reserve Bank of Malawi governor
a4168.speech: Said the deal’s lapse could lead to loss of donor support ; “We have also lost a lot on the funds which could have come with the programme as we only received about $30 million because we couldn’t meet the targets. IMF works with a signalling effect institutions like the World Bank, European Union and other development partners and in the absence of the programme, these will also wane.”

a4168.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, Scotland-based Malawian economist
a4168.speech: Said the lapse may worsen foreign exchange shortages and delay economic recovery, as the ECF was supporting essential imports and macroeconomic stability.

a4168.speaker: Dalitso Kubalasa, public finance management consultant
a4168.speech: Observed that the lapse will further heighten social pressure as citizens already reeling under the high cost of living and struggling to make ends meet may lose hope; while political tensions may rise ; said in the absence of a clear home-grown economic solution, public frustration could further deepen, risking citizens’ hopelessness.

a4323.speaker: Amobi Godwin Ogah, Chairman of the House Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
a4323.speech: Disclosed at a pre-World TB Day press conference in Abuja that the Federal Government has allocated a record N700 billion to fight HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and immunization: “This allocation is a game-changer in our fight against TB and other deadly diseases,” ; commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for prioritizing health funding, particularly in the wake of the withdrawal of U.S. financial support for Nigeria’s HIV/AIDS, TB, and malaria programs: “This is a wake-up call for us as a nation to take full responsibility for our healthcare system and ensure that funds meant for intervention programs are judiciously utilized.”

a4323.speaker: Amobi Godwin Ogah, Chairman of the House Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
a4323.speech: Warned that “One untreated TB patient can infect up to 15 others in a year,” stressing the need for increased screening and treatment initiatives; revealed that the House Committee is working to establish a private-sector-driven TB trust fund similar to existing HIV and malaria funds and is advocating for the Global Fund to increase its TB allocation from 18% to at least 30%: “We will also ensure the passage of a law protecting TB patients from discrimination and stigmatization.”

a4323.speaker: 2024 Global TB Report
a4323.speech: According to the report, Nigeria remains Africa’s highest TB-burdened country, with an estimated 499,000 new cases annually.

a4323.speaker: Dr. Godwin Ntadom, Director of Public Health, Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare
a4323.speech: Emphasised that tuberculosis drives many families into poverty, exacerbated by malnutrition, overcrowding and poor access to healthcare, and that despite 79% of TB cases identified in 2024 receiving treatment, many cases remain undetected, sustaining transmission; noted that a particular concern is the rise in multidrug-resistant TB cases, necessitating targeted screening, better access to diagnostic tools and stronger preventive strategies, especially among children.

a4323.speaker: Dr. Labaran Shehu, National Coordinator, National Tuberculosis, Leprosy and Buruli Ulcer Control Program
a4323.speech: Described Nigeria’s TB crisis as alarming, with 71,000 deaths in 2023 accounting for 18% of TB-related deaths across Africa: “Every hour, eight Nigerians die from tuberculosis,” ; highlighted the severe financial burden on TB patients, with 71% spending over 20% of household income on treatment and 23% resorting to selling property; said funding remains grossly inadequate with only 30% of the required budget met in 2023, cautioning that “Relying on international aid is unsustainable,” and calling for increased domestic financing ; noted progress in expanded TB testing facilities, deployment of 370 portable digital X-ray machines and an improved case detection gap, and urged stakeholders including the media to intensify advocacy.

a4323.speaker: National TB survey
a4323.speech: A national survey revealed that 64% of women and 70% of men either lack TB awareness or hold incorrect beliefs about the disease.

a4323.speaker: Dr. Queen Ogbuji-Ladipo, Acting Board Chair, Stop TB Partnership Nigeria
a4323.speech: In her welcome address, called for stronger commitments from policymakers and increased healthcare financing to accelerate TB eradication, highlighting milestones including the investiture of Nigeria’s First Lady as Global Stop TB Champion, commitments from governors’ wives as state-level TB champions, $50 million in TB funding pledges from government and the private sector, new diagnostic tools including 25 TB LAMP devices from the Nigerian Navy and 50 from private donors, and increased state-level TB budget allocations: “The Pre-World TB Conference is an opportunity to push for policy reforms, service integration, and increased domestic funding,” ; “Our collective action is the key to making Nigeria TB-free. Yes, we can end TB. We fit do am!”

a4323.speaker: Dr. Enang Oyama, Chairman of the Planning Committee for the 2025 World TB Day
a4323.speech: Acknowledged the challenges in organizing this year’s event, particularly due to shifts in U.S. foreign aid policy, but assured that critical activities have been secured: “It is a delight to commemorate this year’s World TB Day under the theme, ‘Yes, We Can End TB: Commit, Invest, and Deliver’,” ; “This slogan calls for urgency and accountability from everyone.” ; thanked the National TB and Leprosy Control Program and partners for filling funding gaps through donations and urged: “As we prepare for World TB Day on March 24, I encourage all stakeholders to actively participate and sustain the fight against TB.”

a4360.speaker: Leila Jewel Djansi, award-winning American-based Ghanaian movie producer (Facebook post)
a4360.speech: Described the Ghanaian movie industry as a “mirthless joke” and urged industry players to take criticisms in good faith to help grow the industry rather than countering these criticisms with knee-jerk reactions ; “Stop enduring mediocrity, please. Instead of these knee-jerk reactions, instead of acting like people just want to hate, forget the who and the how and actually listen. Sit with the criticism. Use it to rise,” she wrote on Facebook ; “Sometimes, when you are given criticism, don’t just get angry and fail to actually see the import or ask the reason behind the accusation. Separate your emotions and be objective,” she added.

a4360.speaker: Leila Jewel Djansi, award-winning American-based Ghanaian movie producer
a4360.speech: Recounted an instance when actor and politician John Dumelo was nearly stabbed on set because a production designer was not careful: “Should I talk about the production designer who passed a real knife to an actor for a stabbing scene? My God. If it wasn’t for divine intervention, Vanessa Williams would have stabbed John Dumelo with a real knife that day. How is this not a joke?”

a4459.speaker: Chadian authorities
a4459.speech: According to the authorities, between June and August nearly 3.7 million people in Chad risk finding themselves in severe food insecurity.

a4564.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4564.speech: Emphasised the critical role of African leaders in steering their nations towards prosperity amidst mounting challenges and underscored the need for collaborative and inclusive leadership to achieve the aspirations of the people they serve ; “We have a mammoth task before us to lead our people to greater heights. Our nations are facing a plethora of challenges. Let us work hard to create an enabling environment that will be inclusive and not leave anyone behind.”

a4564.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4564.speech: Reflected on productive discussions with Ghana's president in Accra, where the signing of a Joint Bilateral Commission signaled a commitment to deepen cooperation in sectors such as education, ICT, health and agriculture, noting these collaborations are vital for fostering mutual progress and aligning with continental frameworks like AfCFTA.

a4564.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4564.speech: Expressed gratitude for the warm hospitality of the people of Ghana, whom he described as embodying “love through kindness and hospitality”, and highlighted the deep ties between Eswatini and Ghana: “Since our arrival, we have been amazed by the love and kindness from the leadership of Kumasi and the populace. We feel at home away from home”, noting Ghana's reputation as the “land of gold and island of peace.”

a4564.speaker: King Mswati III of Eswatini
a4564.speech: Lauded the Ashanti Kingdom's efforts to preserve its cultural heritage and emphasised the importance of safeguarding traditional values while embracing modernity: “Chiefs play a key role in providing appropriate advice to royalty. Such architecture is critical to balance modernity and our traditions” ; praised the unique cultural practices displayed at the grand durbar and urged: “As Africans, we must guide and protect our nationhood and God-given cultural practices.”

a4564.speaker: King of the Ashanti people (Asantehene)
a4564.speech: Addressed the banquet and called for unified leadership solutions to challenges facing mankind, particularly in Africa.

a4576.speaker: Ussene Isse, Mozambican Health Minister
a4576.speech: Announced that the country has medicines available for the next nine months, although there are challenges in distributing them across the country. "Before the US announcements, we had medicines available for nine months" ; "In terms of the quantity of medicines, we are comfortable. But now the challenge is for the medicine to reach the patients. This pillar is fundamental and we all have to collaborate so that the medicine reaches the patients".

a4576.speaker: Ussene Isse, Mozambican Health Minister
a4576.speech: Challenged the factories to produce more medicines in order to reduce the country's dependence on foreign aid and provide medicines for the National Health System. "I've come to the conclusion that we have the conditions in the country to solve the main health problems, because there is a production line for medicines here that responds to our country's disease profile. These factories will be able to export to neighboring countries, because they have quality".

a4576.speaker: Data cited by the Portuguese News Agency Lusa
a4576.speech: According to data cited by Lusa, Mozambique was the member of the Community of Portuguese Speaking Countries (CPLP) that received the most aid from USAID in 2023, totalling over 664 million dollars.

a5218.speaker: Somaliland Quality Control Commission (SQCC) (directive)
a5218.speech: issued a directive banning the importation of empty packaging materials, following reports of traders using empty containers to repackage expired food with falsified expiration dates; under the new regulations, businesses may only import up to 2% spare packaging with their shipments to replace damaged containers, and companies are prohibited from repackaging any food or other products without prior approval from the commission.

a5218.speaker: Somaliland officials
a5218.speech: say the measure aims to safeguard public health and prevent consumer deception ; warn that companies found violating the regulations will face legal action under Law No. 68/2014, Article 45, and that businesses caught repackaging food without authorization could be fined, have their licenses revoked, or face criminal prosecution.

a5218.speaker: Mukhtar Mohamed Cali, Somaliland Quality Control Commission chairman
a5218.speech: “This is a serious public health concern. Repackaging expired food is not only deceptive but also dangerous. No company is allowed to repackage goods without official approval.”

a5218.speaker: Somaliland Quality Control Commission (statement)
a5218.speech: “Consumers have a right to safe, properly labelled food. We encourage them to remain vigilant and report any violations.”

a5221.speaker: One resident of al-Fashir (anonymous)
a5221.speech: “The RSF’s artillery and drones are shelling al-Fashir morning and night” ; added that electricity was completely shut down, bakeries were closed and medical supplies were scarce ; “The number of people dying has increased every day and the cemeteries are expanding.”

a5221.speaker: One doctor in al-Fashir (anonymous, asked not to be named for her safety)
a5221.speech: said hunger was an even bigger problem than the shelling: “The children are malnourished, the adults are malnourished. Even today, I haven’t had any breakfast because I can’t find anything.”

a5221.speaker: Locals/residents of al-Fashir
a5221.speech: said the RSF has blocked food supplies and that aid convoys trying to reach the city have been attacked; told Reuters that many people have resorted to eating hay or ambaz, a type of animal feed made out of peanut shells.

a5221.speaker: One advocacy group
a5221.speech: said even ambaz was running out.

a5221.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a5221.speech: did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a5221.speaker: Enaam Abdallah, 19-year-old displaced resident
a5221.speech: “We fled to Shagra (village) first before getting to Tawila and they attacked us again” ; “If they find your phone, they take it. Money, they take it. A donkey or anything, they’ll take it. They killed people in front of us and kidnapped girls in front of us.”

a5221.speaker: Emergency Lawyers, a human rights group
a5221.speech: said on Monday that at least 14 people fleeing al-Fashir were killed and dozens injured when they were attacked in a village along the route.

a5221.speaker: People who arrived in Tawila
a5221.speech: told Reuters they receive small amounts of grain, including sorghum and rice, but the amounts vary and are insufficient.

a5221.speaker: Médecins Sans Frontières spokesperson
a5221.speech: told Reuters that since mid-June the aid group has treated 2,500 cases of cholera.

a5221.speaker: Coordinating Committee for Displaced People, a Sudanese advocacy group
a5221.speech: said some 52 people have died from the disease.

a5221.speaker: Norwegian Refugee Council (assessment)
a5221.speech: found that only 10% of people in Tawila had reliable access to water, and even fewer had access to latrines; the organisation said most families report eating one meal a day or less.

a5221.speaker: Huda Ali, mother-of-four displaced in Tawila
a5221.speech: “We don’t have houses to protect us from the rain and we don’t have tarps. We have to wait for the rain to stop for the children to sleep” ; said she tried to make sure her children washed their hands and only ate food that had been properly heated.

a5221.speaker: United Nations
a5221.speech: called for a humanitarian pause to fighting in al-Fashir last month as the rainy season began.

a5221.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a5221.speech: rejected the United Nations’ call for a humanitarian pause.

a5236.speaker: Dr Eva Matiko, Director of Projects, Tanzania Health Promotion Support (THPS)
a5236.speech: speaking to the media during World AIDS Day commemorations at the Majimaji grounds in Songea, said THPS provided HIV testing services to 89,602 people in prisons, with 2,030 found to be infected, between October 2023 and September 2024, and that the testing, done through the USAID Police and Prisons Healthcare project, also identified 1,362 people with tuberculosis who were given appropriate treatment; she said THPS achieved this with funding from the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) through the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) in collaboration with the Government ; "Through that project, 2,697 people were started on and completed preventive medication against tuberculosis, including people living with HIV and children under five who were living with people with tuberculosis" ; said that in the same period, through the PEPFAR/CDC Afya Hatua project, THPS provided counselling and HIV testing services to a total of 1,170,902 people, of whom 17,989 were found to have the virus, and that between July and September 2024, 190,311 people received antiretroviral services through 350 health facilities funded by the project ; "Likewise, 1,731 people completed preventive treatment against tuberculosis, and 67,914 women living with HIV received cervical cancer screening services in the regions of Kigoma, Pwani, Shinyanga and Tanga".

a5236.speaker: Dr Eva Matiko, Director of Projects, Tanzania Health Promotion Support (THPS)
a5236.speech: said THPS has planned to provide services to victims of gender-based violence and violence against children ; "This project provided counselling and HIV testing services to 52,978 victims, of whom 47,633 were victims of physical or emotional abuse and 5,345 were victims of sexual violence" ; said they provided voluntary medical male circumcision services to 165,711 men in the Kigoma and Shinyanga regions ; "33,313 adolescent girls and young women benefited from the DREAMS programme in Shinyanga Region, which aims to provide health services and prevent infection among girls and young women."

a5236.speaker: Patricia Kuya, National AIDS Control Programme officer responsible for youth services, Ministry of Health (NASHCoP)
a5236.speech: urged parents to begin speaking with their children openly and to stop being afraid on the pretext of customs and traditions; she said statistics show that young people aged nine to 24 are the group leading in new HIV infections; she said the education provided to parents, young people, community-level service providers, community leaders and teachers has helped educate parents about the fight against AIDS and to keep them from engaging in risky sexual behaviour so as to protect them from infection; she said 350,000 parents and young people from 18 councils in five regions of the country have already been reached and the intervention has been well received, and that it will help parents educate children and young people on how to protect themselves from sexually transmitted infections, hepatitis and risky behaviours continuing in the community such as drug use, smoking and alcohol.

a5236.speaker: Leticia Mourice, Chairperson of the Council of People Living with HIV (NACOPHA)
a5236.speech: called on the community to change its behaviour, to fight stigma, to recognise and defend all those who are sexually abused, and to recognise and fight every kind of social barrier that endangers various groups; she said NACOPHA's efforts continue to be strengthened by ensuring that all groups with special needs are reached.

a5303.speaker: La Releve (Moroccan newspaper)
a5303.speech: indicates that the establishment of textile production units draws on the country's strengths: a skilled workforce, access to European and African markets, and an environment favourable to investment. This project will help increase production capacity, transmit know-how and structure a more competitive industrial fabric.

a5303.speaker: Lopinion.ma, citing the Russian press agency TASS
a5303.speech: the truck manufacturer Kamaz is showing growing interest in the Moroccan market; the company wishes to strengthen its presence on the African continent by exploring new outlets, including the Kingdom.

a5303.speaker: TSA Algerie
a5303.speech: reports that after stabilising at around 250 dinars at the end of February, the euro rose again on the black market to trade at 253.5 dinars at Square Port-Said in Algiers; by contrast, the dollar fell to 241.5 dinars, compared with 243 dinars on 6 March.

a5303.speaker: El Bilad (Algerian newspaper)
a5303.speech: according to it, a trader in Djelfa was sentenced to seven years in prison and a fine of two million dinars for illegal speculation on coffee. The man had been arrested for selling the commodity at an excessive price and stockpiling a large quantity with the aim of creating a shortage. He was tried in an immediate appearance procedure.

a5303.speaker: Business News (Tunisian outlet)
a5303.speech: returns to the official fall in inflation, which has dropped below 6% for the first time since 2021; however, many Tunisians perceive a continuing deterioration in their purchasing power, the gap between the INS figures and reality being attributed to an obsolete consumption basket used to calculate the price index.

a5303.speaker: Libyan Express, citing Africa Intelligence
a5303.speech: announces that USAID has notified its partners in North Africa, including Libya, of the suspension of all ongoing projects. The $50 million in aid approved in October 2024 is frozen. The programmes concerned covered governance, the fight against disinformation and support for young entrepreneurs in the Fezzan.

a5303.speaker: Libya Herald
a5303.speech: according to it, the governor of the Central Bank of Libya, Naji Issa, has ordered card payment commissions to be reduced to less than 1% for all sectors. He also called for the opening of the cash withdrawal service via payment terminals. These measures were announced during a meeting with the heads of commercial banks in Tripoli.

a5303.speaker: Naji Issa, Governor of the Central Bank of Libya
a5303.speech: ordered card payment commissions to be reduced to less than 1% for all sectors and called for the opening of the cash withdrawal service via payment terminals, announced during a meeting with the heads of commercial banks in Tripoli.

a5303.speaker: Daily News Egypt
a5303.speech: notes that Edita Food Industries recorded 33.2% revenue growth in 2024, reaching 16.1 billion Egyptian pounds; net profit stood at 1.4 billion pounds, thanks to growth in all segments, notably biscuits (+144.4%), cakes (+37.1%), wafers (+60.8%) and candies (+57.6%).

a5303.speaker: Egypt Today
a5303.speech: indicates that 100,897 visitors have registered on the digital platform of the General Secretariat of Mental Health and Addiction Treatment since its launch in March 2022; the initiative is part of the Egyptian Health Ministry's efforts to strengthen access to psychological support and awareness of mental health issues.

a5305.speaker: Centre for Research on Multinational Corporations (SOMO) and ActionAid Ghana (report)
a5305.speech: A new report exposes how World Bank-backed projects have prioritised corporate profits while draining Ghana's public funds; the report finds that instead of fostering sustainable growth, the Bank has locked the country into crippling debt, energy insecurity, and fossil fuel dependency, and that all energy contracts that shift financial risk onto the country must be reassessed, with an independent process to assess fossil-related debt followed by cancellation of that debt as part of the IMF-led restructuring.

a5305.speaker: Joseph Wilde-Ramsing, acting Executive Director of SOMO
a5305.speech: "The World Bank claims to champion development. In Ghana, it has done the opposite—fueling debt while ensuring corporate profits come before public need" ; "Ghanaians are paying high prices for electricity they can't afford, while foreign oil and gas companies reap guaranteed profits." ; "Instead of guiding Ghana towards sustainable energy solutions, the World Bank has locked the country into disastrous, high-risk contracts that benefit fossil fuel corporations at the expense of the people. This is utter negligence, exploitation, and a climate disaster rolled into one."

a5305.speaker: John Nkaw, Country Director of ActionAid Ghana
a5305.speech: "Ghana has been compelled to enter into energy agreements that are unaffordable and unsustainable" ; "These contracts seem to guarantee profits for oil giants while our government struggles to pay off debts. The burden falls on ordinary Ghanaians, who must endure high electricity prices while the promised energy benefits remain unfulfilled."

a5392.speaker: World Bank, Uganda Economic Update (report)
a5392.speech: Uganda’s economy grew by 6.8 percent in the nine months to March 2025 on the back of strong performance in agriculture, manufacturing and construction, according to the latest Uganda Economic Update released by the World Bank ; the report projects a positive medium-term outlook, with growth accelerating to 10.4% in the 2026/27 financial year “as oil production begins before stabilising around six percent” ; the report warned of mounting risks to long-term stability: “Oil production timing remains uncertain including completion of large infrastructure, such as the crude oil export pipeline, needed to bring the product to market and generate revenues.” ; the report urges reforms to broaden the tax base, improve equity and strengthen spending efficiency, recommending adjusting income tax brackets, tightening corporate exemptions and reducing wasteful public administration costs.

a5392.speaker: Francisca Ayodeji Akala, World Bank Country Manager
a5392.speech: “Increased election-related spending and declining overseas aid make it urgent for Uganda to boost domestic revenues and curb unplanned expenditures” ; “Increased spending this current election cycle, and with public debt-to-GDP reaching almost 53 percent, raises uncertainties and requires authorities to minimise unplanned expenditures and increase effectiveness in generating domestic revenues rather than cutting development spending” ; “Moreover, considering recent cuts in Overseas Development Assistance, raising domestic revenues has become even more critical, as only then can the government ensure sustained and adequate public spending on key social services, particularly health and education.”

a5488.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a5488.speech: Has announced a significant investment of US$2.5 billion toward the development of key infrastructure projects in Tanzania, with more than 70% allocated specifically to the improvement of roads, railways, and airports.

a5488.speaker: Eng. Mumina Wa-Kyendo, Chief Transport Engineer at the AfDB Tanzania Country Office
a5488.speech: Revealed that the funding would support several major projects, including the Tanzanian section of the multinational Tanzania/Kenya 400-kilometer road, which is currently under construction ; "The Tanzanian stretch of the Bagamoyo-Pangani-Tanga-Horohoro/Lunga Lunga-Mombasa-Malindi road is a critical project. Once completed, it will reduce the travel distance between Dar es Salaam and Tanga by approximately 90 kilometers, saving over one hour of travel time."

a5488.speaker: Eng. Mumina Wa-Kyendo, Chief Transport Engineer at the AfDB Tanzania Country Office
a5488.speech: Emphasized that AfDB's funding is contingent on the effective execution of these infrastructure projects, which are vital to enhancing regional trade and integration; highlighted successful examples, such as the Arusha-Namanga-Athi River and Arusha-Holili/Taveta-Voi roads, which were completed on time and within budget ; "The development of transport infrastructure is essential for regional trade and cooperation. We need to ensure that transport works seamlessly across borders, with roads and railways built to the highest standards."

a5488.speaker: Eng. Robert Achieng, Director of Infrastructure at the EAC Secretariat (speaking on behalf of EAC Secretary General Hon. Veronica M. Nduva)
a5488.speech: Outlined the EAC's focus on developing key multinational corridors in the region, including the Central Corridor (Dar es Salaam-Morogoro-Dodoma-Kigoma), the Northern Corridor (Mombasa-Nairobi-Kigali-Juba), and the LAPSSET corridor linking Lamu, South Sudan, and Ethiopia.

a5488.speaker: Eng. Robert Achieng, Director of Infrastructure at the EAC Secretariat
a5488.speech: Noted that the development of these transport networks is being funded through both national revenues and external development assistance from the AfDB and other partners.

a5711.speaker: Afrobarometer (most recent survey)
a5711.speech: Found that unemployment consistently ranks as the top concern among Ghanaians, with 41 percent identifying it as their primary worry.

a5711.speaker: The Ghana Compact for Political and Economic Transformation (document)
a5711.speech: Highlights key challenges around the employment crisis, including a persistent skills mismatch, an educational system that operates in silos, and graduates ill-prepared for the workforce.

a5711.speaker: KY Amoako, convenor of the Ghana Compact
a5711.speech: Described the proposed National Convention as sending a much-needed powerful message of 'unity, resolve, and commitment to a prosperous, peaceful future'.

a5715.speaker: MCA-Benin (Letter of Invitation / Request for Proposals)
a5715.speech: States that this Request for Proposals follows the General Procurement Notice published on the official websites of MCA-Benin and dgMarket on 27 May 2008 and on UNDB Online on 3 June 2008; that MCA-Benin now invites proposals with a view to selecting a Consultant for the training of Arbitrators, Mediators/Conciliators and staff of the CAMeC, and intends to sign a lump-sum contract for the services; that a Consultant will be selected in accordance with the Quality- and Cost-Based Selection (QCBS) method; and that proposals must be submitted no later than Monday 13 October 2008 at 10:00 a.m. local Cotonou time.

a5715.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation and the Government of the Republic of Benin (grant Agreement)
a5715.speech: The MCC and the Government of Benin have concluded a Millennium Challenge Account grant assistance agreement in order to promote the acceleration of Benin's economic growth and thereby reduce poverty in the country, amounting to a sum not to exceed 307,298,040 US dollars; payments made by MCA-Benin will be subject in all respects to the terms and conditions of the Agreement, including the restrictive rules on use and the conditions for disbursement of the MCC Funds.

a5715.speaker: Simon Pierre Adovelande, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin
a5715.speech: Signs the letter of invitation, asking recipients to confirm in writing receipt of the letter of invitation at the address given: "Please accept, Ladies/Gentlemen, the assurance of our highest consideration."

a5754.speaker: Prof. Wilberforce Sefakor Dzisah, Chairman of the Governing Council of the University of Media, Arts and Communication (UniMAC)
a5754.speech: In his acceptance speech, expressed gratitude to President Mahama and the Minister of Education for the trust and confidence in him and his colleagues through this appointment: "I do not take this honour lightly, but on behalf of my colleague Members of the Council, we appreciate the weight of the responsibility that comes with it".

a5754.speaker: Prof. Wilberforce Sefakor Dzisah, Chairman of the UniMAC Governing Council
a5754.speech: Noted that UniMAC is a "unique institution - one that sits at the intersection of creativity, technology, culture, and information. In a time when truth is often contested, when digital disruption redefines our ways of living, and when cultural narratives shape national identity, our university holds the key to preparing the next generation of storytellers, journalists, artists, policy thinkers, and innovators."

a5754.speaker: Prof. Wilberforce Sefakor Dzisah, Chairman of the UniMAC Governing Council
a5754.speech: Assured stakeholders of the Governing Council's commitment to working collaboratively to deal with UniMAC's infrastructural challenges, promote cutting-edge research, uphold and strengthen academic freedom, and ensure prudent financial governance; touched on strategic priorities including tailoring UniMAC's curriculum to be more responsive to industry and national development, empowerment of faculty and staff, the development of students into ethical, critical thinkers and creators, and the preservation and promotion of Ghanaian culture through the arts and media: "Let us work with urgency, unity, and purpose. On behalf of my colleague Members, I want to assure all of you that we would lead with integrity, transparency, and vision. I welcome the guidance and support of every stakeholder as we embark on this journey together to reset Ghana by adopting bold, creative, resilient, and progressive policies".

a5936.speaker: World Bank
a5936.speech: Has called on Malawi to urgently transition from a government-led to a private sector–driven growth model, warning that continued reliance on public spending will not deliver the structural transformation.

a5936.speaker: Firas Raad, World Bank country manager
a5936.speech: Said in an interview on Friday in Lilongwe that the country's economic stagnation, as evidenced by five consecutive years of negative per capita growth, calls for bold reforms and renewed focus on private capital mobilisation: “This country has been stuck in low-growth equilibrium for decades. In 2025, we are no longer in a low-growth situation; we are experiencing negative per capita growth. Given the high debt, inflation and macroeconomic instability, the only viable path forward is to incentivise private investment, both domestic and international.”

a5936.speaker: Firas Raad, World Bank country manager
a5936.speech: Highlighted energy and mining as priority sectors for reform, adding that boosting energy supply can support industrialisation, job creation and value addition while mining can emerge as a major source of foreign exchange: “Reforming the energy sector to improve supply will be crucial for supporting industrial growth, which is vital for job creation and value addition.”

a5936.speaker: Firas Raad, World Bank country manager
a5936.speech: Cautioned that short-term fixes such as currency devaluation are insufficient to resolve the country's chronic foreign exchange shortages, and instead advocated for a shift from consumption- and import-driven growth to a model anchored in production, investment, and exports.

a5936.speaker: International Monetary Fund (data)
a5936.speech: Data from the IMF shows that Malawi's economic growth has remained sluggish over the past five years, with GDP growth rates of one percent in 2020, rebounding to 4.6 percent in 2021, before falling to 0.9 percent in 2022, 1.5 percent in 2023 and 1.8 percent in 2024.

a5936.speaker: Malawi Government (forecast)
a5936.speech: Growth is forecast to rebound to four percent in 2025, according to the Malawi Government forecast.

a5936.speaker: Daisy Kambalame, chief executive officer of the Malawi Confederation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry
a5936.speech: Said in an interview that the new instruments offer a chance to channel private investment into high-impact sectors: “If we operationalise what is in these documents and national growth and development blueprints, then we can ensure that our investment is targeted to catalytic interventions in critical sectors such as agriculture, tourism and mining.”

a5936.speaker: Vitumbiko Mumba, Minister of Trade and Industry
a5936.speech: Said government will expedite implementation of action plans to ensure meaningful outcomes.

a5936.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a5936.speech: Indicates that Malawi has struggled to sustain growth for decades, despite large inflows of official development assistance, and says that over the past three years the situation has been particularly difficult, with stagnating growth and widening macroeconomic imbalance due to unsustainable debt and the lingering effects of multiple shocks such as natural disasters and the Covid-19 pandemic.

a5942.speaker: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Policy Note 53 (report)
a5942.speech: Reveals how a sudden suspension of U.S. foreign assistance has sent Malawi spiraling into its worst humanitarian crisis in decades, with nearly half a million citizens expected to fall into extreme poverty by year's end and critical health services collapsing nationwide; the cuts total $177 million, or 59% of annual American aid ; findings include 4,451 healthcare workers laid off, 18 HIV treatment centers shuttered, and life-saving maternal health programs nearly eliminated; the aid suspension has slashed Malawi's foreign currency reserves by an amount equivalent to 6.3% of annual imports; the health sector received 57% of U.S. assistance, HIV/AIDS programs have lost 36-39% of funding, maternal and child health initiatives were virtually erased with 96-100% reductions, and agricultural programs have been slashed by 59%; the report warns the double blow of health system collapse and looming food shortages could create a humanitarian catastrophe.

a5942.speaker: IFPRI economists (projection)
a5942.speech: Project Malawi's GDP will shrink by 127 million this year alone, with cumulative losses reaching 1.3 billion by 2030, and that an additional 435,000 Malawians will sink below the poverty line in 2025.

a5942.speaker: Dr. Grace Mwale, a physician in Lilongwe
a5942.speech: “These aren't just numbers in a report – these are mothers who can't get prenatal care, HIV patients turned away from clinics, and children going hungry. We're watching years of progress unravel before our eyes.”

a5942.speaker: Jan Duchoslav, report co-author, IFPRI
a5942.speech: “This aid wasn't charity – it was keeping people alive. The data shows that without urgent intervention, we'll see needless deaths from preventable causes in the coming months.”

a5942.speaker: Esther Phiri, 32-year-old resident of the village of Ntcheu
a5942.speech: “I pray every night that someone will help us. But the numbers in this report show that help is disappearing when we need it most.”

a5978.speaker: Dambisa Moyo, author of "Dead Aid: Why Aid is Not Working and How There is a Better Way for Africa"
a5978.speech: Presents a scathing critique of this approach, arguing that it's not only ineffective but actually harmful to the continent's development. At the heart of Moyo's argument is the notion that foreign aid creates a culture of dependency in Africa: by relying on external assistance, African governments are less accountable to their citizens and more focused on securing aid dollars ; Moyo contends that corruption in aid perpetuates poverty and inequality, rather than alleviating them ; Moyo's argument emphasizes the need for a more nuanced approach to aid, one that prioritizes sustainable development and local capacity building.

a5978.speaker: Dambisa Moyo, author of "Dead Aid"
a5978.speech: Suggests that African countries should focus on increasing trade with emerging economies to stimulate economic growth ; as Moyo argues, it's time to rethink the way we approach development in Africa and focus on creating long-term prosperity through investment, trade, and entrepreneurship.

a6017.speaker: Experts (LUANAR researchers)
a6017.speech: Have highlighted the high cost of smartphones and lack of access to the internet as some of the challenges hindering integration and promotion of digital transmission of extension services to smallholder farmers in Malawi.

a6017.speaker: Dr. Robertson Khataza, Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources (LUANAR) lecturer
a6017.speech: Disclosed that farmers are enthusiastic about digital solutions but that the majority of farmers are not able to buy phones or radios due to limited resources: "Embracing digital advisory services is important in complementing traditional face-to-face extension, which can often be limited by logistical challenges. Digital agricultural advisory and marketing services increase knowledge outcomes and in turn increase productivity, market participation, and ensure social inclusion."

a6017.speaker: Dr. Robertson Khataza, LUANAR lecturer
a6017.speech: Stated that because of lack of information, sellers/farmers fail to find competitive prices for their produce while buyers cannot find quality produce for sale in their markets, prompting farmers to sell in thin rural spot markets or travel to peri-urban markets without information about demand or market price (blind marketing): "Farmers incur significant travel costs, and sometimes fail to register substantial sales (spoilage). Buyers/Vendors struggle to find a consistent source of supply: supply fluctuations, low price offers, stockouts and loss of revenue. Productivity and quality challenges can be worse with limited extension support."

a6017.speaker: Chisomo Haswell
a6017.speech: Said ICT platforms are enabling farmers to share knowledge and experiences on multipurpose agroforestry tree species (MPTS) and other agricultural topics ; Stated that modern ICT platforms can enhance and supplement traditional in-person agricultural advisory services, saying this is why the study was conducted to see how ICT-based knowledge transmission can promote the adoption of MPTS among farmers.

a6017.speaker: Matilda Mtambo, Chief Agriculture Officer for Dedza
a6017.speech: Said digital tools have helped extension workers to reach more farmers with advice on various services and assured that her office will ensure the platforms are sustained so that more farmers benefit: "As you are aware, the government is hit by that high staff turnover, and this has helped us to get in touch with the farmers even when we are far apart. Through digital platforms, the farmers were able to get the right messages for them to continue with agriculture issues in terms of extension."

a6087.speaker: Victor Mapunga, founder of Shona Prince Technologies and authorised Starlink retailer
a6087.speech: "Our goal is simple but bold," Mapunga told The Financial Gazette. "We want to connect one million African homes in the next three to five years. For us, internet access is not a luxury-it's a foundation for education, commerce, and even basic dignity."

a6087.speaker: Victor Mapunga, founder of Shona Prince Technologies
a6087.speech: "We were surprised at first. But it shows that rural Zimbabweans and small towns are hungry for connectivity-they've just never had the option before." ; insists that the real story is in underserved communities.

a6087.speaker: Victor Mapunga, founder of Shona Prince Technologies
a6087.speech: "When people can walk into our shops, it builds confidence. They know they can get face-to-face support, not just an email from abroad." ; "Yes, our revenues are front-loaded today. But we're building an ecosystem: local financing options, community agents, and eventually subscription-based services designed specifically for African realities."

a6087.speaker: Victor Mapunga, founder of Shona Prince Technologies
a6087.speech: "In Africa, you can't just import Silicon Valley models. You have to design for the informal economy, patchy infrastructure, and regulatory uncertainty. FlexID taught me to build from first principles."

a6087.speaker: Victor Mapunga, founder of Shona Prince Technologies
a6087.speech: "When a rural school connects to Starlink, you don't just give them Wi-Fi-you give them access to the world's knowledge. When a farmer checks weather updates or a trader sells across borders, livelihoods are transformed. That's the scale of impact we're chasing."

a6087.speaker: Victor Mapunga, founder of Shona Prince Technologies
a6087.speech: "I don't believe in the founder-as-saviour story. Leadership means creating systems that can outlast me. If Shona Prince only succeeds because of Victor, then we've failed." ; "If ten years from now a kid in rural Zimbabwe can code, learn, or trade globally because we connected their home-that will be enough." ; "We want history to say Africa didn't wait to be saved. We built the future ourselves, one connected home at a time."

a6132.speaker: Hilda Katema Kausiwa, Senior Administrative and Operations Manager, Department of Refugees (Homeland Ministry, Malawi)
a6132.speech: Said the exercise is aimed at finding out actual Mozambican nationals to be residing in the camps to be established ; said the assessment exercise will run for three days from 28th to 30th December 2024 ; “This is going to assist us to identify the needs of the displaced persons and to involve stakeholders for assistance” ; according to Kausiwa, the department intends to relocate the Mozambicans to one camp from the area of Senior Chief Tengani to Nyamithuthu for easier monitoring and supply of humanitarian assistance to the refugees.

a6151.speaker: Report of the joint assessment mission and minimum expenditure basket survey
a6151.speech: According to the report, nine in ten households are unable to meet their livelihood needs, and half of the refugees surveyed are unable to meet their basic food needs. The report also highlights that refugee households are more likely to experience food shortages compared to Namibian citizens. Female-headed households are more likely to experience food shortages compared to their male counterparts, with 82% facing poor or borderline poor food consumption, while 74% of male-headed households face similar challenges. Contributing factors to poor food consumption include limited economic opportunities and depleted food rations. Monthly rations often last between fourteen and twenty-one days, and irregular or delayed distributions due to budget cuts are common.

a6151.speaker: Monique Ekoko, UNHCR representative for the South Africa Multi-Country Office
a6151.speech: "The findings of the report are quite alarming. We are committed to ensuring that the basic needs of refugees are met while promoting their integration into the broader national development plans." ; "Our joint advocacy and resource mobilisation strategy with the government aims to secure vital humanitarian assistance, including food and livelihood support, based on the gaps identified in the current system."

a6151.speaker: Report of the joint assessment mission and minimum expenditure basket survey
a6151.speech: The report points towards the benefits of transitioning to cash transfers to enable refugees to purchase their own goods, both food and non-food essentials, and lays out a strategy to provide targeted food assistance for refugees and highlights the need to create avenues for economic empowerment through skill development and employment opportunities within and beyond the camp.

a6162.speaker: International Energy Agency (IEA), 2015 report
a6162.speech: According to a 2015 report by the International Energy Agency, the world may need to do away with 80 per cent of coal deposits, 50 per cent of oil reserves and 40 per cent of gas deposits without extraction in order to reduce carbon emissions to tolerable levels.

a6162.speaker: United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
a6162.speech: Defined climate change as “a long-term change in the average weather patterns that have come to define Earth’s local, regional and global climates.”

a6162.speaker: UNICEF Report (2022)
a6162.speech: Cited that about 1.5 million children needed humanitarian assistance due to devastating floods that affected 34 out of 36 states.

a6162.speaker: Reuters (13 November 2024 report)
a6162.speech: Reported that heavy rains and floods ruined more than 1.5 million hectares of farmland in Nigeria.

a6162.speaker: Member of the Nigerian Delegation at COP29 (unnamed)
a6162.speech: Informed an audience that more than 40 million people in the Niger Delta had been adversely affected by sea level rise with a huge chunk of land lost.

a6162.speaker: Rural Electrification Agency (REA)
a6162.speech: According to the REA, about 86 million Nigerians lack access to grid electricity, one of the highest numbers by global standards.

a6162.speaker: Governor of Oyo State
a6162.speech: During the inauguration of the first phase of the 11 megawatt Ibadan Hybrid Power Plant Project, stated that the state was aiming at a 500 megawatt solar power generation project to meet domestic needs and sell to neighbouring countries.

a6162.speaker: Kashim Shettima, Nigerian Vice President
a6162.speech: Stated on 19 March 2024 that the Nigerian Sovereign Wealth Fund planned to build a 20 megawatt solar power plant, a first step towards an ambitious 300 megawatt project.

a6162.speaker: ThisDay (review report, June 2024)
a6162.speech: Indicated that the Nigeria Sovereign Insurance Authority had completed the development and construction of a 10 megawatt solar energy project in Kumbotso Local Government Area in Kano State; the report also highlighted several ongoing solar energy projects, including the 5,600 megawatt Argungu Solar Energy Park in Kebbi State, expected to come on stream in 2027, the 1,000 megawatt Jigawa Solar Project and the 350 megawatt Lafia Solar Project.

a6162.speaker: Studies (unspecified)
a6162.speech: Studies have shown that projects associated with renewable energy are projected to create more jobs than fossil fuel energy sources.

a6162.speaker: Gulf Times (3 November 2024 report)
a6162.speech: Posited that Qatar’s LNG production will rise by 35% in 2027, as additional demands from Europe are expected, which would raise the per capita income of the Gulf country in excess of $80,000.

a6162.speaker: Reports (unspecified projections)
a6162.speech: Reports project that lithium demand will rise from 720,000 metric tonnes in 2022 to 3.2 million metric tonnes by 2030.

a6162.speaker: Bloomberg (21 November 2024 report)
a6162.speech: Highlighted that Kuwait proposed to spend over $33 billion to ramp up oil production capacity, placing a bet on increased demand for decades to come.

a6187.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Mozambique (press release)
a6187.speech: Said the United States Government, through USAID, is providing $450,000 (approximately 29 million meticais) to support emergency aid efforts in response to Tropical Cyclone Chido; said the critical funding will help address the urgent needs of affected populations in Cabo Delgado province, focusing on shelter, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH); said one of the grants will be implemented by the Adventist Development and Relief Agency (ADRA), while other rapid response actions will be carried out by CARE International; noted that other USAID humanitarian partners are mobilising existing resources to meet immediate needs; indicated in initial reports that the greatest human and material losses occurred in the southern part of Cabo Delgado province and surrounding areas.

a6187.speaker: Peter H. Vrooman, U.S. Ambassador to Mozambique
a6187.speech: Emphasised the importance of swift action to assist those affected by Cyclone Chido: "The United States Government recognises the enormous challenges faced by those affected and wants to reaffirm our solidarity. Our assistance will provide vital aid to the people most impacted by the cyclone, helping to alleviate human suffering and support recovery efforts."

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: She began: “My purpose of coming here is to give my mother a voice, which was never heard, and never respected. Everything was stripped away from her because there was a system set up to hold her down. It wasn't about a particular government, but a system. She lived as if she was never, ever first lady of Liberia. No benefits, no pensions, no privileges, no acknowledgments. Her diplomatic passport was stripped from her, and she died with an ordinary passport because there were systems and barriers put in place. Only a president could have intervened in her case?”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: She continued: “The second reason is to reveal how Zoe Pennue was instrumental in the demise of my mother. Not only was he instrumental in tormenting her while she was alive, he is going out of his way for us not to have a burial. It's not the government, it's Zoe Emmanuel Pennue. He tormented that lady for so long. Even after her death Zoe is still being a menace in her burial process.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: Said she doesn't have any gripe with the former Liberian leader, rather she was taken aback by the manner in which he tried to portray her late mother as a liar, and for the suggestive manner in which he asked her to come to his place when he visited the late Mrs. Doe's compound to sympathize with the family. “I had never met the former President before. All I expected from him was to say he was sorry because it's at funerals that people bury their hatchets. I just really wanted him to say sorry about the treatment of my mom, not so much for me. A simple sorry would have done it. But when the conversation started, it was implied that my mother was a liar, because he was saying that he met her three times, when in fact it was only one time... That's when I turned around and spoke to the Ambassador Isaac Nyenaboe that I can't accept his gift.” ; “What really broke the camel's back was when former president Weah turned to me and said, ‘I thought you were coming to my place.’ ... So I reechoed that I wouldn't accept the gift, and he said ‘ok’. What I didn't want to do was to cause an embarrassment.”

a6342.speaker: Stanton Witherspoon, host of Spoon TV Live Talk Show
a6342.speech: Asked, “Who told you to go and visit with the former president?” ; “Who brought up this discussion that you should consider going to Weah's place?”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: She answered: “I don't want to go into that, but a lot of things were probably thrown out there in terms of scheduling... This was someone who I had never ever met, and besides, given the current environment, I am the one who's bereaved; I don't go anywhere. I stay in my house.” ; “Well, it's my uncle Isaac Nyenebo, because he's the one making all these arrangements, multitasking with the government. So I didn't take it in bad faith. The reason I objected was because I had never met this person, and also, I am the one who is grieving. You can't go to someone's house and present yourself as the grieving child. I never entertained it, and never thought much of it. I don't think it was done in bad faith, but I was already annoyed.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: Said former president Weah is not her enemy, and she would have appreciated his presence even more if her mother had been alive, because Mrs. Nancy Doe always held the former President in the highest esteem. “President Weah is not my enemy. Zoe Pennue is” ; “We want former President Weah as an ally and a friend; we want him to be ok... I even said to him, ‘I really wish my mom was here, because her sitting next to you now would have made her day. And he said, ‘ok, I understand’. She and my father loved him so much... Former President Weah is not my enemy. I believe everything has been influenced by Zoe. So, I cannot be here calling governments' names because I know what the source was: and it was Zoe Pennue.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: Said with an unhidden tinge of bitterness: “I am sure people always wanted to help my mother but Zoe Pennue has blocked her. In addition to the systems that have been against her, Zoe has been the enforcer. He's truly evil. Because we're first cousins, people from his side visit us. And they would say, ‘when we heard that your mother had passed away, Zoe was celebrating. He was happy. He said, unless Veronica Mamie Doe comes and holds my feet, I am going to make sure that no one from the government talks to her...’ So, he was celebrating. I know how much he was tormenting her. I banned him to not come to the wake, to not come to the burial. Stay away from us because you caused this.”

a6342.speaker: Zoe Emmanuel Pennue, Grand Gedeh County Representative (quoted second-hand by relatives)
a6342.speech: Relatives from his side of the family are quoted as reporting that he said: “unless Veronica Mamie Doe comes and holds my feet, I am going to make sure that no one from the government talks to her. I am going to make sure no one acknowledges her because I have power over these governments. He said, let them go and bury her at Center Street at night.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: She added also: “Zoe's mother is my father's oldest sister. So, we are first cousins. The last time I spoke to Zoe was 2023 because he's always having family reconciliation, and also he has my father's documents. He promised my mother in 2023 to bring my father's documents. He promised to help my mom with the court cases, the ones with Varney Sherman, Vamoma, ECOWAS, that he would ensure everything was settled in one month... He gave my mother $300 to buy white sheep and kill it in her yard... My mom was definitely ill that night. She thought she was going to die. She said she felt like she was being roasted on fire. She couldn't breathe and called her pastor who said, ‘I thought I told you not to go’.” ; “So the pastor told her to go to Zoe's house, get on her knees and beg him to release her... He returned and came back and said, I have released you small... that's how she felt better and I brought her back to England right away. From that day she never recovered.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: Further narrated during the Spoon TV show: “When my mom returned to Liberia in 2004 she was approached by now Senator Edwin Snowe. I think the government was doing renovations on houses that were bombed during the war. So he came to her and said, ‘Mrs. Doe, I am from the LPRC and we'd like to do an estimate’. He sent an engineer to her house and they looked at it and said it was about US$37,000, and he said, ‘sure, we're going to do it’. The next week no one came, so she called him... He said, ‘sorry, ma. You have to talk to your son, Zoe Pennue. I don't want to be involved in family business’.” ; “And then, prior to that, during the Amos Sawyer administration, he said the Doe family should come and claim his cars and stuff. And Zoe, no one nominated him, went ahead and claimed all of our cars. He was driving the white cars, the red cars. When we used to see Zoe, he used to be wearing our father's clothes.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: “For my family and I, our only enemy is Zoe Emmanuel Pennue. He is wicked to the core. Now that she has died, he is still being disruptive, and that is not right. I need people to know what Zoe is saying that everyone is under his control. That's the real reason I am here. I couldn't wait until the burial because that would have been pointless. The Grand Gedeh Legislative Caucus and the representatives have been rallying around me with support. I am grateful for that. And also in America, they are doing the fundraising knowing how my mom was treated.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: “What I learned from the elders is that they knew what my mom what going through; they knew what Zoe was doing but they couldn't do anything. And I am asking why? They would say this to me one-on-one in confidence, but when they congregate, it's like they side with Zoe; except for Ambassador Nyenebo... The properties don't belong to him. The things you hear in these Nollywood movies is what my life has become. Zoe has used other actors in the government and weaponized them against us.” ; “Those traditionalists, where were they when uncle Chayee took my mother to court saying that she wasn't the First Lady of Liberia? It was like a two-year battle. They sat and told me forget it and leave it to God, knowing very well they don't know God. They are demanding that I apologize to Zoe. And I am thinking, in your dreams. Apart from Zoe Pennue, we don't have any grievances. I have no enemies apart from Zoe of course.”

a6342.speaker: Veronica Mamie Doe, daughter of former President Samuel Kanyon Doe and former first lady Nancy Bohn Doe
a6342.speech: According to Mamie Doe, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, his Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, and even former President Weah have shown exceptional concern about the Doe Family plight during this period of their bereavement. “When Vice President Koung called me I was in the UK, this was before I travelled. He called me to sympathize with me on behalf of the government... he asked me to call Zoe Pennue, to which I said it was a no-go.
